a12a.1142756.text: Yeah. No, wait a minute. (Realizing that they have skipped a couple of steps) Excuse me. (Reading) "PLSS diverter Min."

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. [The control for the PLSS diverter valve is located on the bottom-right-front corner of the PLSS and controls the rate at which cooling water flows through the heat exchanger in the PLSS sublimator. They won't start the separate flow of sublimator feedwater until the hatch is open, because the sublimator will only function in a very high vacuum.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: PLSS pump on. [They will now circulate cooling water through a network of tubes woven into the Liquid-Cooled Garments ( LCGs ) which they are wearing over their underwear.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Wait; wait. Let me read that thing (the cue card). (Pause) 115:01:08 Conrad: Come on, let's get the oxygen.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. [Because his suit has collapsed around him, Pete is eager to turn on the flow of PLSS oxygen and get the suit inflated.] [Conrad, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "There's one other thing that should be added to the checklist. When we went over completely on (to) the PLSSs, there was a period of time when you reconfigured the cockpit before you turned on your PLSS O2. The reason you don't turn on your PLSS O2 is that you are going to pressurize your suit (and that would restrict your movements). What happened was that I suddenly realized that both Al and I were in the grip of a great oc

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Wait a minute; get your (PLSS water) pump on. (Pause) [This pump circulates water from a closed-loop supply through the LCG . Flow of the separate supply of sublimator feedwater won't be started until the hatch is open.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: There we go. (Reading) "Diverter Min. Press Regs A and B, Egress"

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. [Oxygen is provided to the cabin either through the Suit Gas Diverter Valve in the ECS suit circuit or through a redundant pair of demand regulators . With the regulators set in the Egress position, there will be no flow of oxygen through them into the cabin when the dump valve is opened. Note that Al has taken over the task of checklist reading.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: (Garbled) (Pause) Okay; they're Egress.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. Now, "PLSS O2, On". [In his eagerness to get his suit inflated, Pete has skipped the step "Verify EVA CB Configuration".]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. (Reading) "Verify..." (Giving in) Okay; that's a good idea. (Pause) There you go.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay; I got an O-flag (and) a tone on. [Before depressurizing the cabin, they will inflate their suits to check for leaks. At first, they will get a warning tone and a warning flag on the RCU . The pressure flag, which should have been showing all this time, should clear at 3.1 to 3.4 pounds per square inch (psi). The oxygen flag and tone should clear at 3.7 to 4.0 psi. Once those clear, Pete and Al will turn their PLSS oxygen off and watch the rate of pressure decay. They expect a decrease of less then 0.3 psi in one minute due to breathe-down (carbon dioxide removed by the PLSS LiOH canister

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: (Keeping an eye on the step they have skipped in the checklist) Okay; check your CB configuration while we wait.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: I don't think we can both turn around at the same time.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Okay, go ahead and check yours and then I'll check mine. (Pause) [Among other reasons, they are checking the circuit breakers to make sure that nothing got accidentally hit with the corner of a PLSS. This was a recurring problem, despite the fact that the switches and circuit breakers were protected with guards. There wasn't much spare room in the spacecraft when they both had their PLSSs on.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: How's your (foggy) window doing?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: It's clearing up. (Pause) Okay; looking good. Run my suit press(ure) up. (Pause) (The pressure is) coming on up. (Pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: You wanted to do the (pressure integrity) check now?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Yeah.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. (Pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: It feels good in this one-sixth g, doesn't it?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Yeah, except I notice that, with the slight slope we're standing on, I keep falling in the back.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Uh-huh.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: I think I got my oxygen off. (Pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Coming up. (Pause) [They are doing the one-minute pressure integrity check but, unlike later crews, will not report the results to Houston.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Those rocks having been waiting four-and-a-half billion years for us to come grab them.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Think so, huh?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: (Laughing) Let's go grab a few.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: (We've got to) get an ALSEP out first.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: (Laughing) Okay. (Garbled) the old (pressure) check.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay; mine's holding real good. (Static; pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: You got a good tight suit?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Yep. (Pause) And the tone came off, so I really did have the oxygen off. I've got a good tight suit. [Although Pete is referring to a good pressure check, his suit actually is too tight and the fit will cause him problems, particularly during the sleep period. See the discussion after 122:37:27 .]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Houston, are we Go for EVA?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1142756.text: Stand by, Intrepid. We'll be right with you. (Pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: (Acknowledging Gibson) Okay.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: "Stand by?"! You guys ought to be spring-loaded.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1142756.text: Intrepid. You're Go for EVA.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Roger. (To Al, reading) Cabin Repress valve - Closed.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. Just a second. [The final means by which the cabin can be repressurized is through the repress valve. Al has to turn to reach the valve, which is at about waist height on the front face of the ECS behind him.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Easy does it.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Cabin Repress (pause), Closed. [They are now ready for cabin depressurization.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. (Reading) " Dump valve Open, then Auto at 3-1/2."

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. (Pause) [Al is reaching down to get the dump valve . There is also a dump valve in the overhead, rendezvous hatch. Although the checklist calls for use of the hatch valve, the choice of which valve to use for depressurization is up to the crew. Because it is a bit of a stretch to reach the overhead valve, only relatively tall people like Charlie Duke (183 cm) on 16 and Gene Cernan (183 cm) on 17 used it. Neil Armstrong (180 cm) opened the Apollo overhead valve for the depressurization prior to the post-EVA equipment jettison. During final preparations for Apollo 14 EVA-1, Ed Mitchell sug

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Easy does it. (Pause) Want me to help you?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Nope. (Pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: What do you need?

a12a.1142756.text: Just need to move a little bit.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Okay. (Pause)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Kind of give me a push back, Pete. (Pause) [The handle on the hatch is on the lefthand side and the dump valve is on the righthand side. With his suit inflated, Al is having trouble reaching the valve in the crowded confines of the LM. He seems to be saying that, while he can get down low enough, he is overshooting his mark and needs Pete to push his shoulders toward the right side of the spacecraft so that he can grab the valve.]

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Why don't you let me get it? Al? Stand up. Stand up, Al.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: I got it. The lock (means "handle")'s in the way again.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Yeah. Why don't you...Wait; you're going to tire yourself out doing that. (Pause) Let me get it. (Pause) That a boy. (Sound of depressurization can be heard) Okay. That's it. (Watching the pressure gauge) Cabin going down. Okay.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Mark. 3.5. Okay?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1142756.text: Copy 3.5.

a12a.1142756.text: Let me see. "(Reading) Verify cuff gauge does not drop below 4.8."

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean
a12a.1142756.text: Sure doesn't.

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: Man, mine's up in the overhead someplace. (Pause) [Pete means that his suit pressure is very high. Prior to the partial cabin depress, they had inflated their suits to a relative pressure of about 3.7 psi. Now that they have dropped the cabin pressure from 5.0 psi to 3.5 psi, the relative suit pressure has increased to about 5.2 psi and will now decrease due a combination of (1) the suit pressure relief valve which opens at relative pressures above 5.0 psi and closes again at 4.6 psi, and (2) breathe-down.] RealAudio Clip (6 min 13 sec)

a12a.1142756.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1142756.text: You got a foggy visor?

a12a.1142756.speaker: Bean

To prevent overheating the MESA cavity and to conserve electric power, the TV is normally off. CB(16) (Circuit Breaker Panel 16) is on Al's side of the spacecraft.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Got it, Houston. (Pete giggles) That's beautiful. That's too much.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1164100.text: Well done, troops.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: I gotta go put the...

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: We got it, babe! It fits in the RTG real well! It's just the cask was holding it in on the side.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1164100.text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. One minute to LOS.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Don't come to the Moon without a hammer. (Pause) That's it, Pete.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: (Laughing)

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Outstanding! 116:49:52 Conrad: (Laughing; Pause) [Conrad, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "(When we started to off-load the ALSEP), the first thing we noted was that, as soon as we put the packages down on the surface, they began to accumulate dust. Everything went as advertised until Al screwed the cask removal tool on the cask (means the fuel element in the cask) and (it) would not budge. We got the normal fix-it: the hammer. While I beat the blazes out of the side of the container, Al managed to start the (element) out. He'd get a little notch of it every time I'd hit the container. And I

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Let's make our move (and carry the ALSEP out to the deployment site).

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: I'm ready. (Pause)

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: That cask's going (in?). Okay, Houston. The fuel element is in the RTG . I can feel it radiate heat already! (To Pete) Put your hand over here.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1164100.text: Copied that, Al.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Wait a minute; don't move...No, wait a minute, Al. Have you got a strap around your boot? Let me look and see.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: No. You're all right.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: All right?

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Yeah.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Boy, this thermal coating doesn't mean a thing here (because it gets dirty so quickly).

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Uh-huh. That thing is really getting covered with dirt.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Gosh! I hope they made allowances for it.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Me, too. Okay. [The thermal coating that Al is referring to is the reflective, white-cloth covering on the packages. As mentioned previously, any dirt that gets on the covers will increase the amount of sunlight absorbed and, therefore, the internal temperatures of the various pieces of equipment. He is hoping that the designers took into account the possibility that the equipment would get dirty and would get hotter than if it stayed clean.] [Next, Al attaches the ALSEP packages to the carry bar. Getting the packages properly locked onto the carrybar was always a problem and, on Apollo 16, on

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. You're in, pal.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: It doesn't look like it (is properly attached). Let me look at that just a second.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Okay.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: It's the right way. (Pause)

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: That's it. [Bean - "The trouble was in lining it up. You had to line up the package perpendicular to the shaft to the nearest degree and you couldn't ever do it. That was a hard job to do. We needed a better alignment way to click those in. In fact, when I carried it out, it fell off once, didn't it? They had little over-center holders and you'd hit a bump and it would come right out. 'Cause the thing was (flexing and) bending. When I carried that baby out, it was like carrying springs. In training, we just carried makeshift ones and the pole was stiffer."] [Each end of the carry bar has a fla

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Hey, feel the heat off that machine. That's amazing. 116:50:59 Conrad: 1400 degrees (Fahrenheit or about 760 Celsius). (In a conspiratorial tone) Almost as hot as the Sun! (Chuckles) [Conrad - "I must have taken this picture (AS12-46- 6791 ) just about the time you hooked up the RTG . You've got your hand over the side and that's when you're talking about the heat, because your hand is right next to the radiator."] [Pete also took 6792 about this time.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Hey, do me a favor. [Al is ready to start carrying the ALSEP and wants Pete's help in getting his hands properly positioned. The problem is one of not really being able to see something so low and close while, at the same time, trying to get low enough to grab the bar. On Apollo 16 and 17, Duke and Schmitt, respectively, generally bent forward to grab the bar and then, as they lifted the packages, ran forward to get it under control. Al may be trying to do a more controlled, static lift.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: What do you need? No, go lower. There you go. You got it.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Okay; let me go scout...smoke over the area. [Pete is saying that he'll go out west of the spacecraft and look over the potential deployment area. They need to be at least 300 feet from the LM to minimize the amount of dust blown onto the experiments during launch. The reason that they will do the deployment west of the LM is that, shortly after lift-off, the spacecraft will tilt toward the west - so that it can catch up with the orbiting Command Module - and, as a result, will blow most of the dust toward the east.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. Got everything you need?

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: (Examining his cuff checklist entry at 1+36 ) All right, there's no TV, so I got the SIDE (subpallet) and the picker-uppers for the rocks (meaning the tongs)!

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. [Had the TV still been working at this point, Pete would have now pointed it at the planned deployment site. Pete removed the SIDE experiment from the RTG package at 116:41:29 and will handcarry it out to the deployment site. This is the "subpallet" item on his checklist. The "picker-upper" is a pair of tongs that he got from the MESA at some time since they started the ALSEP off load.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. Let's go right off to our little mound over there; how does that grab you? [There are two conical mounds of dirt near the ALSEP deployment site. Evidently, they have already noticed the larger of the two. They did not, however, mention the mound during the site description they did prior to the EVA preps. Thomas Scwagmeier has created a composite from views out each of the windows and one of the maps that show the large mound.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. Now, something's wrong.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: What's the matter? (Long Pause, probably while they make sure the packages are secure on the carrybar)

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Well, it's kinda...The thing doesn't...Well, let's try it.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1164100.text: Pete, we copy. You've got the UHT, tongs, and (SIDE) subpallet.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: We're making our move, Houston. I can tell this is going to be a workload. I'll take it easy.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: (To Houston) How long did you say our shadow was...(that is), the LM's shadow, 150 feet?

a12a.1164100.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1164100.text: Stand by, Pete.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: No, that isn't any 150 feet. (Pause) [If the shadow is 150 feet, they'll only have to go twice that far to get to the 300 foot minimum distance.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Take your time, Al; I'll just go on out...

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: That's what I'm doing. What's the hurry? We got it made.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: No, I'm just going out to scout the area, that's all.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay, I'm going to set it down and rest...

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. 116:52:43 Bean: ...and go to intermediate cooling . (Garbled) (Pause) [Al is carrying the ALSEP low, with his arms hanging down. See a detail from Pete's pan frame AS12-46-6806, which he takes at about 116:57:52 .] [Bean - "It was hard to carry that way; it kept bumping your knees. And then your knees would knock and it would rattle and jump."] [Conrad - "Well, it weighed about 300 Earth pounds, so it had a lot of momentum."] [Bean - "On Earth, when they gave us one that weighed like it did on the Moon (that is, a 50 pound mock-up), it had the momentum of the light masses. But you get up

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: You know, they ought to build this equipment for lunar operations some other color besides white.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: (Laughs; Pause) I'm going to go right up to the Head Crater, I guess.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Well, if you're going to do anything...(Pause) Okay; let me move another couple of...

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Got any direction you want me to go?

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Well, it looks to me like either the direction you're headed is good, or the one a little bit more to the right. You're going to have to go far enough so we don't end up in one of the craters when we furthest south deploy.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. (Pause) [They will deploy all of the experiments south of the Central Station and, hence, need to leave themselves enough room between the Central Station and Head Crater to get everything on level ground and in the proper relative position.]

a12a.1164100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1164100.text: But I want to go 10 degrees off our takeoff angle; and I think I'm headed out about that way now.

a12a.1164100.speaker: Bean
a12a.1164100.text: Okay. (Pause) [Presumably, they want to get far enough off the direct LM track to prevent any significant interactions with the engine exhaust.] TV Troubles Apollo 12 Journal ALSEP Deployment

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: You just stay back there and take your time. I'll go out here and scout the area.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: You're getting pretty far out.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Huh?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Getting pretty far out.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Pete and Al, your LM shadow should be about 110 feet.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. I'm looking for...I'm dying to find out what this mound is over here anyhow, Al. (Pause) We got a very peculiar mound sticking up out of the ground, Houston. I want to go look at it. As a matter of fact, I think I'll go take a picture of it. No, my...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Roger, Pete. Could you give me your position and distance with respect to the LM?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Wait one (minute). [The mound, which is actually the larger of two near the ALSEP deployment site, can be seen in the site map at R-4, 13.1. The LM is at Q-5, 15.2. the grid lines are 50 meters apart, so the mound is 114 meters from the LM on an azimuth of 293, which is 23 degrees north of west. Thomas Scwagmeier has created a composite from views out each of the windows and one of the maps that show the large mound. They haven't yet noticed the smaller mound.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Go ahead, Pete. Do what you're doing. (To Gibson) Pete's about...I'd guess, about 300 feet (90 meters) at 12 o'clock (from the LM) in the bottom of a shallow crater that you're bound to see on your map. It's sort of a doublet. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I'm headed to the right-hand edge of the Head Crater.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Roger. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Hey, Al. Here's a neat spot to put it out up here.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Is it flat for a good piece?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Oh, you'd better believe it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. It's a good long ways away too; it must be at least, what, 500 feet from the LM?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I don't know.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: 600? [Analysis of photos taken at the ALSEP site with the LM in the background - an object of known size - indicates that they deployed the Central Station about 130 meters (roughly 430 feet) from the spacecraft.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: It's the world's most peculiar...I got to photograph this thing. I can't imagine what it is. The mound's sticking up; and I can't imagine how it got there or what would make it. (Pause) [Pete takes a down-Sun photo of the mound, AS12-46- 6793 , as he approaches.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: (Probably commenting on Pete's running) Boy, you can cover the ground on this lightweight...at one-sixth g. Really move. 116:55:53 Conrad: I got to get them a stereo of this thing. It's really fantastic! Oops. (Pause) [Once Pete gets close to the mound, he takes a stereopair, 6794 , and 6795 , stepping to his right between frames.] 116:56:04 Conrad: How's our timeline going, Houston?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Pete, at 1 plus 48 into the EVA, you're looking good. Looks as though you're right on there, if you've just about completed your traverse.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: We have, Houston. Yeah. Now, look, Al, look over here.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: We're way out from the LM.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Over here, Al.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: See where I'm headed. This great big flat area.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: That's a good...Hey, there's another one of those mounds over there.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Where? Hey, you're right! What do you suppose they are?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I don't know, Houston, what they are; they're just sort of mounds. Looks like - don't take this the wrong way - it looks like a small volcano, only it's just about 4 feet high and, at the top, it's about 5 feet across; and it then slopes from the top on down to the level with the terrain, and that diameter - that circle where it finally becomes level with the terrain - is about 15 or 20 feet. So it looks sort of like a small volcano. There's a couple of them out here. They look like they were formerly made out of mud or something.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Al, Roger. We copy. [The mounds are described in more detail at 118:10:36 . Al's comment 'Don't take this the wrong way' at 116:56:35 is probably related to a story that Jack Schmitt told me. During Apollo 11, Buzz Aldrin said he saw bright flashes of light at places in the soil - like biotite (a form of mica), he said. He wasn't saying that the material was biotite, only that it flashed as biotite would. According to Schmitt, some geologists were highly critical of Buzz's use of the word - a criticism that Schmitt rejects as being completely unwarranted. Furthermore, Schmitt said that Pete an

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Is there any hole or central vent?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I don't know. I got to go over...We'll go over after we get the ALSEP out. There's a couple of them here. (Pause) This is a...We couldn't ask for a better spot to put this ALSEP down.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: No. This is nice. Hey, (there are a) lot more rocks up here (than there are around the LM).

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (To Houston) Listen, there...We could play geologist for two days and never get any further than we are right now. Seeing all different kinds of things.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Hey, here's a different one. 116:57:52 Conrad: Yeah. It's really neat. Better than any of the geology field trips . Look at that thing. (Laughs) I'm getting a quick pan of the area here to tie down the ALSEP deployment (site). There you go. [The LM will be in at least one of these pictures and the size and orientation of the LM in the image will help in pinning down the ALSEP location.] Pete's ALSEP site pan (frames AS12-46- 6796 to 6811 )

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. Man alive! [Al may have just joined Pete. He left the LM at 116:52:07 and, deducting 44 seconds for his stop to change to Intermediate cooling, made the 130 meter trip in 5 min 20 sec. His speed was a modest 1.5 km/hr.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Tired?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: No, I'm not so tired. That handle, you know, when you carry this thing around in one g, the ALSEP tends to hang down. But you carry it around up here at one-sixth and, particularly, the RTG tends to rotate the whole pallet. So, in a few minutes, you've got one of them kind of half way up in the air and the other one's down by your left leg, being afraid that the handle's going to come undone. You know, the handle doesn't lock. Okay. (Pause) [See Al's comments at 116:52:43 .]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: What happened to all those...Hey, that's slick. You know these neat little decals we got on here?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Uh-huh.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: You can't hardly read them in the sunlight because they don't have enough contrast to them. They're so bright. (Pause) [Bean, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "One thing that turned out a little different than I imagined - I had difficulty reading the decals that we had put on the ALSEP. As I recall, looking at it on the surface (means 'in training'), it looked as if there were black writing on a silver background. When I tried to read this on the lunar surface, it was very difficult. The brilliant light reflected off the silver and you couldn't see the black. We had the sequence of laying th

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay, let's move them. (Pause) Okay. Let me make sure now that we're not going to run out into some holes. (Pause) That's pretty good. Pete, I'm going to move just a little bit further to the east - or, correction - to the north, so that I won't end up over in that hole with the SIDE. Okay?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: All right. [Using his training experience, Al is visualizing where each piece of equipment will go. The planned layout is shown in Figure 3-6 from the Mission Report . He is now on the checklist page that begins with "1+48, System Interconnect". Procedural details can be found on pages 44 and 45 in the Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Operations Plan ( 7 Mb ).]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: And I think it would be a real good spot. (Long Pause) Okay, I'm...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Awfully frustrating. [As indicated below, Pete is having trouble with the SIDE. He is also at 1+48 in his cuff checklist; and is removing the SIDE from the subpallet he handcarried out from the LM.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: And I think this is the spot, Pete, right here. (Pause) Let me look and make sure, now, that we're going to have a good place for everything. Yeah, we will. Magnetometer can sit over there and the seismometer will sit in a good flat place. Although, the trouble with the seismometer (is that) we don't have any good solid bedrock or anything to set it on. All we've got is this dirt. And I don't see any area around that has any rock.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Roger, Al. [Jones - "Were you being literal about rock to set the seismometer on?"] [Conrad - "I think they wanted as hard a surface as possible."] [Bean - "And then we didn't find any. 'Cause we thought we'd maybe see some dirt and some rocks and things, and we were going to set it on a flat piece of rock. But now we're telling them, 'forget it, all we got is dust up here.'"]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I'm afraid we're just going to have to take what we can get on this seismometer. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: You know, there must be some thermal expansion or something. I'm having a heck of a time getting this UHT (Universal Handling Tool) in this SIDE. (Pause) It just flat won't go in there. [Pete may be trying to engage his UHT in a carry socket on the SIDE, turning the UHT into a handle. This is step 'b' under 1+48 on page 44 in the Ops Plan.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Well, just pick it up with your hands. I always handled the SIDE (Suprathermal Ion Detector Experiment) with my hands.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I can't bend down that far.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okey-doke. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Garbled) free. (Long Pause) [Jones - "In one g you could bend down far enough to pick it up?"] [Conrad - "Sure, you could get a little help (from Earth gravity). Especially with a 70 pound PLSS on your back and everything, you could get down. But up there, you strain..."] [Bean - "And you're still way up off the ground."] [Jones - "Could you have done the ALSEP deploy solo?"] [Conrad - "Yep."] [Bean - "Sometimes, when you were training, you'd try it. It wasn't that hard. All you had to do was to be able to read the labels - unscrew the Boyd bolts and read the labels. That was about it."] [Onc

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Ready to take the SIDE cable to the Central Station as per step 'j' .) Where'd you go, Al?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I'm right over here, babe.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Turning) Oh, you're miles away.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah, I am. I moved over here.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Oh, son of a gun! [Apparently, Al has changed his mind about where to put the Central Station and, now, Pete will have to move the SIDE again in order to make an electrical connection. That means engaging the UHT in the carry socket, which has already given him trouble.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I had to do it, Pete, so that I'd have a good place for the (garbled). (Pause) Okay, there's a good spot. Looks good. (Long Pause) [Bean - "It seems to me I set the ALSEP (Central Station) down, and had to go move, for some reason. I don't remember for sure. But that may have been what happened here. It seems to me that, somehow, things didn't look right and I had to move it about three feet."] [Having done the deployment in practice several times, Pete knows how far Al should be from him at this point. Three feet is enough of a move to notice.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Al, when you deploy that PSE (Passive Seismic Experiment) stool , it would help if you tamp that ground down as well as you could before putting the stool down. [Figure 3-1 from the Preliminary Science Report is a schematic diagram of the PSE experiment.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I'm going to try to do that. This ground, you know, it doesn't get hard as you move down a couple of inches. If you tamp it, and that's what I'm planning to do...But I don't know. We'll just have to see what happens. I'm worried about it getting a thermal short myself.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Roger, Al. (Long Pause) [Bean - (From the 1969 Technical Debrief) "The first experiment I put out was the passive seismic. I had two anomalies that I know. One was the skirt (which is discussed below)...the second anomaly (and the first in sequence) was that the little dish the passive seismic sits in needs to have a solid bottom so when it is placed on the ground, there is no danger of dirt easing up through the center of it, as there was in the case of our dish, and touching the bottom of the passive seismic itself and causing a thermal short that would ruin it. We spent quite a bit of time

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Boy, I'll tell you.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Man, are you dirty.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Boy. Sure. (It's from) carrying that ALSEP. Look at the ALSEP.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I know.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Ridiculous (Laughs) I remember how they took care of this white paint. You had to have gloves to touch it. (Pete laughs at the thought; Pause) [NASA photo S69-34035 shows Pete Conrad and Al Bean examining the Passive Seismometer prior to the flight. The fact that they are wearing white gloves, caps, etc suggests that this is the flight hardware and that it wasn't only the white-painted objects that were handled with great care pior to the flight. The object in the foreground is the folded-up Hand Tool Carrier (HTC).] [Bean, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "I think we're kidding ourselves if

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I got a kind of a problem here. (Pause) I'm going to have to do this myself. I'll have to do this backwards; but it's going to work right. (Pause) Oops. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Do me a favor, Pete?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Garbled) I'll be with you in a minute.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: You can relieve me in this SIDE right here while I (garbled), because it looks like it might...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah. Give me that thing. Let me hold it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Easy, easy. That a boy.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I got it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: That a boy. Now, wait. 117:04:20 Bean: Watch for that (garbled) cable.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah, but let me get it plugged in. [Pete is asking Al to hold the SIDE while he plugs its cable into the Central Station. This is the fifth item in the System Interconnect section of his cuff checklist.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: They (the cables) sure splay around under this one-sixth g, don't they? It's moving around a bunch. (Garbled) Watch it, watch it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Where's the orange stripe?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Should be (the) same as on that other one.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Obviously, it's on the side I can't see.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah. Blue to blue. (Long Pause) You know, that noise - that whistling - is coming from you, Pete, because every time you move around, it whistles. When you stop, it quits.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Is that right?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: There it is.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Is it locked good?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yes, sir.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay, here's...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Garbled)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Here's yours.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (We don't want to) drop that baby (the SIDE?).

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. You got it?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Let me have the cable right there.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: All right. Oops! That came out.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: That's what I wanted.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: That's what I wanted. [They may be referring to a lanyard on the SIDE which Pete will pull to release the legs. Pete seems to be doing the deployment step from memory, rather than consulting his checklist. Releasing the SIDE legs is the third item in his 1+48 paragraph.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: All right. Those legs came out nice.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yup. (Pause) The next thing I got to do is head this way with it, right?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: No. Before you do that, come here a second, would you, please?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah, but let me set it down one moment. Uh-oh; the top popped open. [Bean, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "When we were deploying the suprathermal ion detector, the lid came open a couple of times. This lid was supposed to be deployed (by) ground command after we had left the (ALSEP deployment) area so that the exposed, mirrored surface would be nice and clean and the two detectors would not get dust in them. I'm pretty sure that we did get some dust on the top of it. I hope it's not enough to bother the operation."]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Is it) supposed to do that?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: No. Not supposed to do that. You can close it, though, before it gets any dirt in it. You can just reach up there and close it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. You better...You better...(garbled under Al)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: (Garbled under Pete)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: ...close it while I'm holding it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Before we get any dirt on it. Son of a gun. Why did that happen?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Never saw it do it before. (Garbled) We could still salvage that, though.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Wait a minute. The little...The little...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I see it. I see it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: That a boy.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Now kind of turn it over with your other hand, Pete. So...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Wait a minute, (garbled).

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Wrong way.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Where do you want to go with it?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Well, I want to see the...Let me get this. Okay. Now, let's see the other side.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: This way?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: That's a boy. Yeah; this won't hurt a thing. Now...Wait a second. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: That's it. You got it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: But just don't touch that. It'll be okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Didn't hurt a thing.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Let me just put this down here.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. [Compared with later ALSEP deployments, Pete and Al are having more than their share of difficulties. Readers should keep in mind that Neil and Buzz only deployed two scientific instruments - a passive seismometer and a laser retroreflector. Neil and Buzz had some problems with their deployment - for example, a BB leveling device that refused to operate properly for a while - but Pete and Al are really the first crew to do a full ALSEP deployment and, not surprisingly, are discovering a number of design and procedural flaws which didn't manifest themselves in 1g training. As a result of

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Pete, before you set the Central Station down for the final time, if you would also tamp that ground down, it would help in keeping the dirt off of the thermally-sensitive areas.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (To Al) Oh, I did it, I did it. (Laughs)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: You set it down.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Laughing) I set it (meaning the SIDE) down and it didn't fall over. I can't believe it. [Pete has put the SIDE out of the way so that, later on, Al can carry it out 60 feet SSW of the Central Station for final deployment. According to the Apollo 12 Mission Report, the three legs on the SIDE were too close together for good stability and, consequently, the instrument was easy to tip over.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Here I come. What do you need, Al? 117:07:05 Bean: Use your tongs to hold this (probably ALSEP package 2 which is the base for the RTG) up a minute. It (the RTG)'s a little hot, and I don't want to touch it. Watch (out for) this. [Al has asked Pete to help him with the RTG package while he removes the bracket holding the RTG cable and attaches the cable to the Central Station. These are the fourth and fifth items under 1+48 on his checklist page. Details can be found on pages 44 and 45 in the Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Operations Plan .] [Bean - (From the 1969 Technical Debrief) "We had no troubl

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Where are my tongs?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Right there in your...There you got them. Now if you'll just hold it steady, then I can do the rest. (Pause) There, now. That's good. (Pause) Thanks, Pete. Got it. [Pete usually his tongs at his left hip, attached to a spring-operated, self-rewinding device called the yo-yo. The yo-yo operates very much like a rewinding tape measure and lets him carry the tongs without having to use his hands and, then, when he wants to use them, he just reaches across with his right hand and pulls out as much cable as he needs. When he is done with the tongs, he simply releases them and they spring back onto

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. Now we're going to get the easy part.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. Take your time.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Thing's coming out real well. [Al may be referring to the RTG cable.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: The name of the game is to get the ALSEP here. (Running or, at least moving quickly) Whoooom! Up through one crater and over another. (Hearty laugh)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Oh, man.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Does that look as good as it feels?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: It does. Hey, I'll tell you the way to do it. Pete! Tend to rock from side to side as you run. Like that. There you go.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Joyous laugh)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: You really move better that way.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Here I come, ready or not. (Pause) [Evidently, Pete has just run for the first time. He seems to have run for about 20 seconds and is about to return. As discussed after 133:12:31 , during the second EVA after having gained some experience in running, Pete and Al ran about 220 meters eastward from Sharp Crater at an average speed of about 4.0 km/hr, of a bit more than one meter per second. Pete probably didn't run that fast this first time and, consequently, ran no more than 20 meters. Evidently, the SIDE subpallet is some distance from where he has been helping Al.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Houston, I'm not kidding. We are really getting dirty out here. There's no way to handle all this equipment with all the dust on it. Every time you move something, the dust flies; and, in this low gravity, it really takes off. Goes way up in the air and then comes down and lands on you.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: How far do you estimate we're from the LM? 600 feet? 700 feet?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: At least.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I think you're right. 6(00 or) 700 feet. [A traverse map made from low-periapsis Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera photo M168353795R indicates the Central Station is about 126 m (413 feet) from the LM.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: (That's the) way to do it. [It is impossible to know what Pete has just done. Perhaps Al is still watching Pete run. Pete's next checklist item is still connection of the SIDE cable to the Central Station. HIs next transmission indicates that he is not yet at the Central Station.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Here I come. Dee dee, dee dum. (Long Pause) Dum dum, dum dum. Coming after the (Central Station) antenna mast (which had been serving as the carry bar and was left attached to ALSEP Package 1 that includes the Central Station and holds various experiment packages).

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. (Long Pause) Okay. Let me plug this thing (the RTG cable connector) in (the Central Station base), Pete. [After a careful review of audio and the available documentation, it seems to me that it is most likely that Pete plugged the SIDE cable into the Central Station during the Long Pause in the transmission Al just finished. With the cable plugged in Pete tries to reach down to remove the carry bar.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I can't get down low enough to get it (the carry bar) off.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I'll get it for you, if you can't.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. Wait a minute. Let me move that dust cover for you. [They are both working at Package 1. The dust cover in question is probably the Central Station connector dust cover that, as per item "l" near the top of the lefthand column on page 45 in the A12 Lunar Surface Ops Plan, Pete would have removed prior to connecting the SIDE cable. Note that the same item appears as item "m" in Al's list of activities in case he was ready to connect the RTG cable before Pete as ready to connect the SIDE cable. Pete may have simply dropped the cover on the ground and, now, notices that it may be in Al's wa

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: How's that strike you? Okay. (Garbled)...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Hey! Look at that (dust cover) go. (Responding to Al) Strikes me pretty good. I'll be tamping the dirt around this Central Station. [It is impossible to know what Al meant by 'How's that strike you?' or who threw the dust cover. One possibility is that Pete handed it to Al so he had both hands free to deal with the carry bar. Pete is tamping the dirt around the Central Station in preparation for tilting it down onto its base for levelling and alignment.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. (Pause) You're going to have to design things with little legs on them or something, so you can put them down and they stand off the soil. (Laughs)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: If we had that suit we could bend over in, we'd have the job done by now.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Hey, can you push down on this side of that? [Al is having trouble connecting the RTG cable to the Central Station.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yes. My biggest sweat is trying to bend over. Wait a minute. Ready, get set, push. That on, or not?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I don't think so.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I don't think so.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: No, let me look at it a second. Here we are.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Which way do you want this?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Under there.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Under. (Pause) I had to really push that other one (that is, the SIDE cable connector). Look at all that dust! (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay now... (Pause) Wait a second. Wait a second. Let me get it with you. (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Ready? (Pause) That got her.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: That did it, now.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: That did it.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Now we won't touch the shorting button. [The shorting circuit allows current from the RTG to flow through some resistance without going through the experiments. Only when the experiments are all connected will they push the shorting switch and divert the current flow out of the shorting circuit.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: (To Houston) Okay. We've connected the RTG to the Central Station, Houston. And we're ready to go to work deploying the experiments.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I('ve) got the antenna mast.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: All right.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Dee dum, dee dum. (Long Pause) [Pete is putting the antenna mast on the SIDE subpallet, possibly to keep it out of the dust and/or to make it easy to grab later.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Pete, did you experience any trouble with the dust cover on the SIDE?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: It opened, Houston, and we closed it again, and we got no dirt on it, fortunately.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Roger, Pete. Well done. (Long Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. Let me tamp the dirt down underneath the Central Station. Hey, easy does...Whoops! (Laughing) That's me.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: What happened?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Oh, I started to walk away with the Central Station attached to the UHT via the little gizzy.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. The RTG's down and cooking.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. I'm tamping the dirt, here.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Okay. [Pete is probably still tamping down soil to form a base for the Central Station.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Have I got it tamped pretty good? Look over where I'm tamping. How am I doing?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Looks good. Need a little bit more this way, I think. The problem with tamping, Pete, it looks like every time you tamp that, as your foot comes up, you know it...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah, (garbled)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: ...it redusts the area.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah. Okay. (Pause) Here we go, Al. (Pause) Now, take your UHT, there...

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: And move that.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: ...and keep the SIDE cable clear.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Sounds good. [ALSEP package 1 has been standing on edge. The base of package 1 is the Central Station. After they remove the experiment packages, Pete will configure the Central Station by raising the top and, with it, a pre-attached thermal curtain. He will then assemble and aim the antenna. For the moment, Pete and Al are tipping package 1 over onto its base so that they can remove the experiment packages. ]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: All right.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Go, babe.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Here she comes. Over she goes. (Pause) Get it right down the Sun mark. [Knowing where the Sun is supposed to be at this point in the mission, they can use a shadow device to align the package in a predetermined direction so that, later, Pete's antenna alignment job will be relatively straight forward.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: No. There you go.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: How's that?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: That's good.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Ready to go to work. [Al's next task is to deploy the passive seismometer( PSE ).]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Go. Have at it. (Pause) Okay; what have I got. Let's see. I've got to get the solar wind, huh? [Pete's next task is on the checklist page that starts with "1+58, SWE Deploy". Apollo 12 carried two solar wind experiments. The first was the Solar Wind Collector (SWC), the foil "window shade" that Al deployed near the LM at the start of the EVA as per his checklist at 0+57 . That experiment captures solar wind atoms for return to Earth and determination of the relative abundances of the various constituents. The experiment Pete is about to deploy is the Solar Wind Spectrometer - usually referred

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Solar wind. I'm going to do the... (Pause) I better... (Pause)

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Houston, how we doing on the timeline? (No answer; Long Pause) Do you read me. Al?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Sure do.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Hello, Houston. How we doing on the timeline? (No answer; Pause) [They are both at 1 hour 58 minutes in their checklists. They started the final depress at 115:08 and, therefore, they are 2 hours 6 minutes into the EVA. Despite all the problems they have been having, they are only 8 minutes behind schedule.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: They may be talking to Yankee Clipper. (Not true; Pause) 117:14:14 Gibson: Al, did you have a reading on the shorting amps?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Wait a minute. I'll get it. [Houston wants to know how much current is flowing through the shorting circuit. Al's checklist calls for such a report, but he neglected to do it.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Hold the phone. Do you read me, Houston?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Sure do; go ahead.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah; I was asking you how we were doing on the timeline? (No answer; Long Pause) Can't see that (shorting amp) needle anywhere. Can you, Al?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Let me see it. Let me help you. Doesn't it show any amps?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Place is covered with dust.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1165401.text: Pete and Al, at 2 hours and 7 minutes into the EVA, you're about 5 minutes behind.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: (Responding to Gibson) Okay.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Hold me a little bit.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Wait a minute. Going back to Min cooling . What do you need?

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: Hold me and I'll look.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Oh, okay. Easy, don't... (Pause) [Pete may be holding Al's hand while he tries to get close enough to the meter to see the needle. The meter is on the Central Station base and is only a couple of inches off the ground.]

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I don't even see a needle in there.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: I don't either. That's what's bothering me. It's not reading zero, and I don't see a needle.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Bean
a12a.1165401.text: I don't even see a needle in there. Houston.

a12a.1165401.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1165401.text: Yeah. Okay. Let's quit screwing with it. (Pause) (Let's) get on the timeline.

a12a.1172334.text: And, Pete and Al, a comment on picture taking. If you would, try to document some of the dirt which has gotten all over the equipment. If you would, try to get close-ups which will show the dirt we might have on thermally-sensitive areas. And, also, when you get done, if you would, take one or two extra pictures showing the ALSEP with the mounds that you described previously in the background. That'll give us a good geometric reference.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. I did a pan...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Hold that, Pete.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I did a pan out here at the...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Just a second. Now, let me hold this end and you stretch that end out. [They are having trouble getting the CCIG to sit upright because of cable coiling.]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. I got it.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Go to the right. That's it. Get the coils out of it.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Which way's that thing head?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: It's got to head away from the Central Station; away from everything. Probably ought to be a point right over there.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: But, now, I think if you kind of twirled it a couple times, it would end up uncoiling that twist in the line there. (Pause) That's the right way. Try it that way again. Looks like it might be working. (Pause) That's good. That's doing good! Okay. Let me take and set this thing down, and it's supposed to point to the Earth this way. That'll be good.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Get your ground wires wrapped around the legs.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay, I got it. Looks like it's going to be okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1172334.text: Go ahead.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Yankee Clipper, if you'll give us POO and ACCEPT, we'll ship you up a state vector, a target load, and a REFSMMAT.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Put it down.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1172334.text: You('ve) got it.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: (To Dick) Roger.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Hold on; hold on. (Talking to the experiment package) Don't tip over.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah; wait a minute, wait a minute.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I got it steadied.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. [Bean, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "The suprathermal ion detector and the cold cathode ion gauge, which were combined experiments, were difficult to align, and we knew this before we left. The legs (on the SIDE) are too close together for the height and weight of the experiment. When you try to get it on the ground, it just wants to tip over. The little place where you insert the ALSEP tool (the UHT) is on the end that has one leg. It's a three-legged configuration; and, so, that tends to, if you put any offset of force on that attachment, tip it over. The Cold Cathode Ion Gauge co

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: There, that's all right.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Just hold it there just a...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Watch it, watch it, watch it.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. I'm trying to.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: No, your foot's hung in it. That a boy.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: That did it. Okay. Let me sneak it back on again. Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Now, what do you want?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I want to put that (SIDE) lid back on there. (But) it would probably be best if we just left it off.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I think it would be best if you left it alone.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Now, you hold it there (either with his foot or a tool) while I (garbled)...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I got it. I got it anchored.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: ...because this (the CCIG he is manipulating) is going to want to turn it (the SIDE) over.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah. I know.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. We're coming up with a load.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Step on it (either the cable or the CCIG).

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. That's what I think I can do.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Those guys got to be kidding about that cable on the... I knew that thing was going to do that. (Long Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: There, maybe that's better. (Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Come on, this thing's making us run behind.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I know it, but I don't see any way to quickly get...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: (Laughing) All right; now, just a minute. Move your foot. (Pause) That's better.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Let me just try it a couple more times. I think if I hold it this way and use this tool, I can probably set it...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Hey, it's just like zero g; everything floats up. That baby's going to nose dive into the dirt every time, sure as I'm standing here. That cable's cleverly designed to make it do that. [The Apollo 12 Mission Report promised that, for Apollo 14, "the wires of the connecting cable will be tied at 6-inch intervals instead of being tied with heavy Mylar tape. This modification not only reduces cable stiffness by 70 percent - which decreases the spring effect - but also decreases cable bulkiness to permit easier stowage." Despite these changes in the cable configuration, the Apollo 14 crew also had

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Let's put it like this. (Pause) Down like that. 117:53:35 Conrad: Don't fall over.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. (Pause) There's no way (to get it properly oriented).

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Uh-uh. Just... That a boy. (Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: That thing goes right in the dirt each time...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I know, I know. It's going to do that. It's very frustrating. Turn it around and point it the other way. See if it'll point out that way.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: All right. That might be good, too. Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I knew that ding-a-ling cable was going to make us spend hours trying to do that.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: (Laughing) Doesn't that make you mad?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah; I know. Especially when you know it's going to happen.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Look, why can't I set it like this? You just let go of the SIDE and come over and step on that thing.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Hey, if this SIDE falls over, then I'm really going to be mad. I got that thing firmly planted.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Just a minute. Wait, wait. Hold it, hold it. Hold her a minute. Okay. If I can get this just arranged.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: That's it. Now step on it.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I can't. There's no way.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Let go of the string in your hand. That a boy. Now stand...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: It's just...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: (Talking to the equipment) Don't flop. That's it. Push it in.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Ah! We made it. I hope. Let's push it real hard in there.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. [The surface soil is loose enough that it can't provide much lateral restraining force. Tools stuck a few inches into the ground will stand upright but the CCIG has too broad a base to go in very far.]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I think we've got it licked.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: That a boy. Easy does it.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: (As the experiment falls over again) Aw, you... The thing just jumps right up. (Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: (Laughing)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Pete, I'm just afraid that one's... We've had it on this one.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: (Laughing) You've had it on that one, my friend.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Hey, here it is here. Look; I don't think it makes any difference if it lays on its side as long as it points its aperture in the right place.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Let's move it around here and just let it lay on its side. (Pause) You know, it doesn't know the difference. (Pause) Just kind of lay it around. Just try to... Yeah; that'll work; that'll work.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Al, we concur with that. Go ahead.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: That work right there? [The CCIG experiment - which was also called the "Lunar Atmosphere Detector" - was designed to be deployed with its aperture pointed horizontally, away from the LM, in order to minimize the influence of outgassing from the spent descent stage. Although, in the final orientation, the CCIG aperture was pointed mostly upward, it was looking away from the LM and, consequently, the experiment returned useful data. The CCIG essentially measures the density (or, equivalently, the pressure) of the extremely tenuous lunar atmosphere and, as detailed in the Preliminary Science Rep

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: (Responding to Gibson) Okay. It looks like the only way... This cable has just got too much spring for the weight of the package, and there's just no way. Okay, Pete. Let her go. Now, let me level it (the SIDE). (Pause) No way (is the CCIG going to deploy properly). 117:55:54 Conrad: That's a shame. (Pause) (To himself) What time is it, anyhow? (Pause) (To Al) Let me get over here and get a big picture of this. [Pete takes a picture of the Central Station and nearby equipment from a distance of perhaps 25 meters to the southwest. This is AS12-46- 6819 , in which most detail is lost in the glar

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Pete, you're 2 plus 48 into the EVA. (Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I'll level this, Pete. (Pause) It's leveling good. Leveling real good. (Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: That American flag sure looks pretty back here next to the LM, doesn't it? And the S-band?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Looks like a model. 117:56:42 Bean: Okay. I think that's going to do it for the SIDE. That's the tough one. (Looking at his checklist to see what photos he needs to take). (f/)11, one (picture taken) cross-Sun. [Al takes two close-ups of the CCIG - AS12-47- 6922 and 6923 .] 117:56:47 Conrad: Back off; I got the picture.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: You already got a cross-Sun? Can you see the bubble and everything in it?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: No.... 117:56:53 Bean: Let me get it. [Al's close-up of the top of the SIDE is AS12-47- 6924 .] 117:56:56 Conrad: ...I'm just getting one from a distance, here. That a boy. (Pause) (I'll) get (the focus set to ) 74 feet. [Pete takes AS12-46- 6820 of Al getting a close-up and then turns to take a locator shot, 6821 , showing the Central Station.]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Al, copy you have the SIDE deployed?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Yeah. Everything's deployed. I'm going to go get the shorting plug now, Houston.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Standing by.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Dum dum. Dum dum, dum dum. Boy, do I like to run up here. This is neat!

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: It is fun.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: The first thing we've got to do is run over to that volcano-looking... or whatever that little jobber-do is. That's interesting. [Pete is now on his checklist page that starts with "2+25, ALSEP Activation".]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay, Houston. Here comes the shorting plug. (Long Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Yankee Clipper; Houston. The computer is yours.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: (To Houston, partially garbled under Gordon) How about Astro(naut) switch 1?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1172334.text: Yankee Clipper, Roger. [Apparently, Gibson did not hear Pete's question under Gordon's acknowledgment.]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Hey, Al.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Yes, sir.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I need your help over here after a minute.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I'll be there.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Houston, how about Astro switch 1?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: You're clear to rotate Astro switch 1, Pete.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. (Pause)

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [The switch is located at the bottom rear of the Central Station and Pete is probably turning it with his UHT. During the 1991 mission review he said that he wouldn't have been able to get low enough to turn it by hand.]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Gosh, you can't... We('ve) got to re-align that antenna. (Pause) Okay. Houston. Astro switch 1 is rotated. Shorting amp switch is in. I'd be a happy man if you tell me you're getting a signal.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Roger, Pete. Stand by. [Conrad - "I must have moved the station when I turned the switch. And I'm asking him to check the antenna (alignment by checking the signal strength)."]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Boy, it's all put out. It sure looks nice.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: How about messing with this one thing right here?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. I will do it, Pete. Also, I wanted to just look at the numbers (for the CS antenna pointing) with you, too. Hey, just do me a favor. Use your tongs and pick up a couple of these Boyd bolts and set them on the edge of that skirt on the passive seismic. There's about 10 Boyd bolts just near it over there. What did you want me to look at?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Just check that antenna; make sure it's level.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Look; you do that (Boyd bolt task). I'll give you the tongs. I'm going to run over and photograph this ding-a-ling looking (mound)...

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: All right.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Pete and Al.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: ...want to stay out?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: Pete and Al, Houston. Looks like you did the job. We're getting data back.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Hey, Houston. You just don't know how happy I am. [Conrad - (From the 1969 Technical Debrief) "I feel we did most of our homework on the ALSEP."]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Tell me again the numbers you're supposed to use (for the antenna pointing).

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: 16.44/5.25. Here, turn around.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I shouldn't have done that. You're dirty all over, here.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. [Pete has probably given Al the tongs.]

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: All right, I'm going over to this mound.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I'll be back in a flash. Bye-bye.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. I'll tell you the numbers I read; you tell me if they're right.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: Okay.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: I read 52... No, correction, I read 525.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: That's right.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. I also read 16 (pause) 42.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: I don't know what this thing is. It's really weird!

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: 1642. Is that it?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1172334.text: Okay. Same thing. Looks good, looks good. 118:00:46 Conrad: I don't know what this (mound) is. Let me get the (garbled) feet at f/8. a12a.1172334.text: Houston; Clipper. (Long Pause)

a12a.1172334.text: Yankee Clipper; Houston. Go ahead.

a12a.1172334.text: Houston, are you going to have a maneuver pad for me?

a12a.1172334.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1172334.text: That's affirmative. We'll be up with you in about two minutes.

a12a.1172334.text: (Garbled)

a12a.1172334.text: No, I haven't. No, I haven't.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: That's great.

a12a.1172334.text: (Garbled) go. 118:04:01 Conrad: Are you through (with the deployment tasks)? Al? [Gibson has been reading engineering info to Gordon, and Al may have started to take documentation photos of the ALSEP site.]

a12a.1172334.text: Yeah. I got some pictures to take and that's it.

a12a.1172334.text: Hey, Houston; Yankee Clipper.

a12a.1172334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1172334.text: (Garbled under Gordon) and I'll meet you over at that big mound. All right?

a12a.1172334.text: All right.

a12a.1172334.text: Clipper, go ahead.
