a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Intrepid, Houston. Would you give us aft Omni? (No answer) Intrepid, Houston.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: First, would you give us (the) aft Omni (directional antenna)? And we are ready to pick up with the debriefing.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Aft S-band? Is that what you want? (Long Pause)

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Intrepid, negative. That's the VHF antenna.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: (Garbled) (Stops to listen) (Long Pause)

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: And, Intrepid, we're ready to pick up with the debriefing.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay, Houston. Go ahead.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. Two questions related to the mounds which you saw out there. Is the object at R-5, 13.1 a mound or a rock? And, secondly, confirm that you did get a sample of the mound material.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Yes. We got a sample of the mound material; we got lots of them. And would you say again the coordinates?

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Coordinates are R-5, 13.1. (Long Pause) [They may be eating and/or performing the PLSS feedwater recharge.]

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: No. I don't think so, Houston. This mound is too small to show up like that. I believe. I'll look at it a little bit more here for a minute and think about it. The mound... I'll tell you where the mound is. The mound is not seen on the map. What you gave me was a crater. [Pete is wrong about this. The object at R-5, 13.1 is, indeed the larger of the two mounds. The Lunar Orbiter photograph from which the map as made was taken when the Sun was low in the eastern sky. Consequently, a crater which has a shadow on its sunward - up-Sun - side is dark on the east and bright on the west. A mound or r

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. We copy that. And on that mound sample, you got material from the mound as well as material around the mound itself.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: That's right. We can get, tomorrow, a documented sample if you want.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: We will talk to you about that in the briefing before the EVA, Pete. And a question on the number and sizes of rocks. What was the ratio of fines to rocks that you finally ended up with? (Pause) 121:43:03 Conrad: I put two of the large scoops worth of fill (that is, regolith) in one bag that had three rather large rocks in it; I think it's three. And the other bag of rocks fills half of the rock box, and I guess there were, what would you say, Al, 10 (or) 12 rocks in there? And the rock box is full to the top. I couldn't get anything more in there, I'll tell you that, and get the core tube in

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. We copy that. One question on the SIDE dust cover. Was the SIDE dust cover well aligned after reclosing? And the reason for asking that is in case we suspect a misalignment, we would try to activate that now and if it doesn't work, we'd have a manual backup.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Bean
a12a.1213148.text: The SIDE dust cover popped off about three times, Houston. And the last time it popped off was when we just finished aligning it neatly (and) level and we put out the cold cathode ion gauge. And the cover popped off again, and we didn't want to disturb the experiment to try and put the cover back on. We'd spent already overtime on it, so we just left the cover off. So, as the experiment sets right now, the cover is off. Now if this is not acceptable, I guess we can take a swing by there tomorrow and try to put the cover back on. And we can put it on lined up accurately as it was to begin with,

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. Stand by on that, and we'll be massaging that one tonight.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Bean
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. My recommendation is - unless it is going to hurt the SIDE - to leave it just like it is, because it is just a precariously balanced experiment over there and it is going to take time to do it right. [Overnight, the experiment team will decide to leave the experiment alone. Because of the difficulty that Pete and Al had in deploying the SIDE and CCIG, the experimenters don't want to make things worse. The only danger, really, is dust contamination of the experiment during lift-off and, evidently, the experimenters deemed this to be an acceptable risk. In the end, the experiment worked we

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. We copy that, Al. And, Pete, could you give us an estimate of the number of rocks that you have on board?

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: I really didn't get a count, Houston. Well, let me see. I guess it would be about, (to Al) wouldn't you say, about 15 to 20 rocks is all.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. We are looking for really the quantity of rocks, pounds of rocks.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: That rock box is heavy, I'll tell you that. I think it is right up to Max.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. That is good enough. One last question, Al. When you took the fuel element out, in the extraction, what was the force profile like? In other words, did it all of a sudden come free at one point or did it gradually come free as you extracted it? 121:46:16 Bean: Well, Pete started pounding on the side; and, as it came out, an eighth of an inch at a time - make that a sixteenth of an inch at a time - until it was about three-eighths of an inch out. And once it was three-eighths of an inch out, it slid out rather easily.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. We copy that.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: What is the fuel cask made out of?

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: That's graphite.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. Well, I pretty well was beginning to bang it up pretty badly. As a matter of fact, I think I cracked it. I had better go look at it tomorrow. But I was rapping it as hard as I could and was getting about an eighth of an inch at a time until he finally got about, what would you say, Al, an inch and a half out, and then it came all the way.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. (Pause) Pete, no problem with that. You don't have to go back to it.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [As indicated in the discussion from the Mission Report which is reproduced at 116:49:52 , the element came loose after 0.6 inches of travel - about 5/8ths of an inch.]

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Pete, we have a procedure here in order to get the water out of the suit loop. First, (put the) suit loop... (correcting himself) or the Suit Isolation (Valve to) Disconnect, both; (then) disconnect the O2 hoses. (Next, put the) Suit Isolation (valves) to Suit Flow, both; lower the outlet of the hose to floor for about 2 minutes. (After that, put the) Suit Isolation (valves) to Disconnect, both; connect both O2 hoses; (and, finally, put the) Suit Isolation (valves to) Suit Flow, both.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay, I understand that one, and we'll do it in a little bit. We're eating right now. I got my hoses disconnected anyhow.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger, Pete. And we don't see a real easy way of getting the water out of the boots. If you turn the heat way, way up, we may be able to dry some of it out. And the other thing is to use gravity in whatever way you could use it. [Because the inner boots are integral parts of the suits, the only way to completely drain the water would be to take the suits off, something they don't want to do unless absolutely necessary.] [Jones - "What was the main reason for not wanting to take the suits off? Time?"] [Conrad - "We just weren't allowed. It hadn't been cleared yet."] [Bean - "The concern was tha

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: I don't have that much water in there, and it's drying up. Or, at least, it's as warm as I am right now, so it's not bothering me and it's no sweat.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: I just want to make sure the suit loop's running right, that's all.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger, Pete. [See Pete's discussion of the sleep period, which is reproduced at 122:37:27 .]

a12a.1213148.speaker: Bean
a12a.1213148.text: Say, Houston. Question for you.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Go ahead.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Bean
a12a.1213148.text: Here's a question for you, Houston. With the tapemeter being like it is and those erratic readings we seem to be getting approaching PDI, as far as the backup perilune monitor check. How are we going to use that tapemeter tomorrow when we're trying to update the AGS in range and range rate (during rendezvous)?

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: That's a good question, Al. We'll be working on that one. That's another one for tomorrow. We're going to have a lot of people thinking hard over the sleep period.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay, I think we could just call Noun 78 with P20 running. Isn't that right?

a12a.1213148.speaker: Bean
a12a.1213148.text: You could do that...

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: And the first thing that I'd propose doing, Houston, is we'll get a quick airborne check after we launch and I get a manual lock-on or something, go do a Verb 63, and check the tapemeter against the DSKY .

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: That's no big deal.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger, Intrepid. [As Houston will tell the crew in the morning at 129:33:57 , there is nothing wrong with the tapemeter . The 'erratic' readings were due to the fact that numbers in the checklist that they used in making the test were nominal values rather than values appropriate to the actual orbit they were flying. In using the checklist values in an overnight simulation, engineers in Houston reproduced the tapemeter readings observed by the crew.]

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: We recommend, also, that you shoot for the 3-1/2-hour EVA. (Pause) [The checklist contains options for EVA-2 lengths of 3 hours 20 minutes and 3 hours 50 minutes, with the difference being the length of the geology traverse. Given that they are running behind the timeline, Houston is leaning toward the shorter EVA.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 11 min 19 sec ) includes conversation between Ed Gibson and Dick Gordon.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay.

a12a.1213148.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1213148.text: Roger. And we'll wake you up at the nominal time in the flight plan (which is 129:55).

a12a.1213148.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1213148.text: Okay. [Very Long Comm Break; Dick Gordon begins his rest period. PAO announces at 121:59 a change of shift, with Glynn Lunney's team of flight controllers taking over from Gerry Griffin's team. Astronaut Paul Weitz is now CapCom.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 45 min 24 sec ) includes a few seconds of the change of shift press conference. PAO resumes coverage at 122:57 and gives a summary of the following and then plays the accumulated tape. Note that the accumulation was done with a voice-activated taping system.

a12a.1215044.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1215044.text: Roger. And we'll wake you up at the nominal time in the flight plan (which is 129:55).

a12a.1215044.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1215044.text: Okay. [Very Long Comm Break; Dick Gordon begins his rest period. PAO announces at 121:59 a change of shift, with Glynn Lunney's team of flight controllers taking over from Gerry Griffin's team. a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Roger. When do you want us to change the... Give me a time for the (ECS Primary) LiOH cartridge change, would you, please?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. Sure will, Pete. Now we got a couple more questions to get rid of some Irish pennants here; and when you answer these, we can turn you loose to go to sleep. [Conrad - "'Irish pennants' is a navy term. It means that there are some loose ends hanging around. On a ship, if you have Irish pennants, that means lines aren't tended right. They're hanging over the side, they're not coiled correctly, whatever."] 122:13:49 Weitz: First off, what are your intentions for your suit-hose configuration for sleep? Over.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Al says he's hot, and he's going to leave his connected to blow air. I'll probably sleep with mine (his suit hoses) off.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. Understand. Secondly (as per checklist), how about, for our friendly surgeon, a crew status report and a medication and radiation status?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. The crew's in super shape; no medication; and let me look at my little Rad(iation) counter here, just a second.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1221334.text: (Sounding quite stuffy) LMP had one of those decongestant pills just prior to EVA.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Understand, Al.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: And my Rad counter is 11020.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1221334.text: And mine's 04020.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay, thank you. One last question. Did you have any problems with the tapemeter during your descent other than it reading high on the perilune check?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1221334.text: We had it in Altitude/Altitude Rate on the descent, naturally; and it looked to me like it agreed pretty closely with the PGNS's numerical readout on the DSKY . That's what kind of concerns me about the rendezvous radar. Also, that low transmitter power - maybe they're hooked in somehow.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. Thank you.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: I disagree on low transmitter power. We got surface lockup when the command module went by at a good P22. The tapemeter did not run in the P22 like it does in the simulator, I'll say that for it. And secondly, it was off - I don't remember the number now - but it was off from its normal reading in self-test. Although the PGNS portion of rendezvous radar self-test was absolutely correct. So I suspect that there may be just something wrong with that tapemeter. I don't think there's anything wrong with the rendezvous radar itself. [P22 is the radar test program from the surface as the CSM goes ov

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay, thank you. And it was not in agreement; it was not erratic in operation in any way, was it?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Nope; it runs just perfect - not erratic. I think there's just... My impression of these perilune altitude checks, I think, (is that) there may be a bias on it, like 30 or 40 feet per second.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Roger, Intrepid. Thank you. (Long Pause) Intrepid, Houston. Pete, the second time you disconnected your suit hoses, did you get any water out of the hoses then?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Well, it was the second time that I got all the water out of them. I took them off the first time and put them on the floor as advertised and didn't get any water out of them. I put them back on again; I started getting water in my boots, so I took them off that time, and I never put them on the floor; I just took them off and it blew three three-quarter-inch water balls right out of it, that splattered all over the spacecraft. And, since then, it's been pretty good. And we turned the suit-dealie (the suit-circuit temperature control) here up full-hot, and we'll see how that works.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. Thank you. (Long Pause) Intrepid, Houston. Has Al done the same thing with his hoses, Pete? And, if he has not, we would like to request that he do so before you turn in. 122:18:37 Conrad: Yeah, he hasn't gotten any water, but he's going to drain them right now. Now, look, you got us down here for an hour to eat tomorrow. We're in one-sixth g and it doesn't take us anywheres near that long to eat; we can whistle through things a lot faster. I think we can pretty well stick to the nominal timeline and get a good night's rest. It may turn out, that after 6 or 7 hours worth of sleep, we're

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. That will be fine, Pete. [Comm Break]

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Intrepid, Houston. Request that Al go to Suit Flow while he's disconnected so (that), if there is any water in there, it will blow it on out.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1221334.text: (Expressing his pleasure, with perhaps a small hint of sarcasm) That's a pretty reasonable request. [Long Comm Break]

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Hello, Intrepid; Houston. Over.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Go ahead.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. Pete, can we have the results of Al's suit loop check?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Roger. He got two drops of water. That's it.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay; understand. And on that lithium hy(droxide)...

a12a.1221334.speaker: Bean
a12a.1221334.text: It's one of those mysteries of life, Paul. I don't have any water in mine, to speak of, and Pete has his coming out all the time. We've been shifting over to (Water) Separator B, but I really don't think that's the answer. Must be something to do... Just like on Neil's spacecraft with (garbled) hoses or the way it turns or something else. [Except for separate hoses, they are hooked up to the same ECS plumbing, hence the mystery.]

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Roger, Al. Understand. And also, on the lithium hydroxide canister change, if it fits in with your activities at that time, we would like to have it changed out at 130 hours on the clock. And, for your information, you're 12 minutes past the halfway mark in your total mission time.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Roger. And you want the LiOH out at 130:00?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: That's affirmative. (Long Pause) Intrepid, Houston. Let us know when you're getting ready to turn in, Pete, and we won't bother you any more. 122:31:39 Conrad: Okay. We're still doodling around here a little bit; we're just getting ready to rig the hammocks now.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Roger.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Al wanted to go EVA again, and I restrained him until tomorrow.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. Good show. [Long Comm Break] [Jones - "The hammocks showed up after 11? Or were they going to be on board 12 from earlier than that?"] [Conrad - "We were the first ones who were going to sleep. They didn't sleep, did they?"] [Jones - "Neil and Buzz had a rest period, but they just kind of curled up in corners."] [Bean - "The hammocks were always there (for Apollo 12), as far as I know. We always were going to have them. There wasn't any last minute thought 'Well, hey, we gotta give you somewhere to sleep'. I think we always knew we were having hammocks."] [Conrad - "Didn't we invent them

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Say, Houston, do you want us to go to Down Voice, Backup and Power Amplifier, Off?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Stand by there, Intrepid. (Pause) Intrepid, Houston. That's affirmative, Pete.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Okay. We're going Down Voice, Backup and Power Amplifier, Off, at this time and configuring for sleep.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: Roger, Pete. Nighty-night.

a12a.1221334.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1221334.text: Okay, and I understand 129:55 is reveille (as per checklist). Is that right?

a12a.1221334.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1221334.text: That's affirmative. [Reveille is 7 hours, 18 minutes from now.] 122:37:27 Conrad: Okay. We'll gauge it on that. Nighty-night. [PAO resumes live coverage after completing the playback at about 123:06.] [Pete will sleep in a hammock stretched out fore and aft, as close to the ceiling as it can be hung and still give him some room. As per Surf-64 , after they get both hammocks hooked up, Pete moves to the raised, aft part of the cabin to get out of Al's way while he gets in his hammock. Then Pete gets in his hammock.] [Bean - "One comment I would make: if I did it over again, I would take a sleep

a12a.1285100.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1285100.text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid. How are you this morning?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid. How are you this morning?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Good morning, Intrepid. How did you sleep?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Short, but sweet. We're hustling right now, and we're going to eat breakfast, have a little talk with you, and get about our business.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Sounds good. [Comm Break] [Bean - (Laughing) "It's a typical Conrad operation. 'We'll keep you informed; we're way ahead of it. We're going to do it.'"] [Conrad - "'Yeah, and don't bother us.'"] [Bean - "'Check in with us. We'll be ahead of this. We'll get going.' It's a classic Conrad statement."]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Houston, Intrepid. What's the local time down there, Paul?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: It's 19:25 now, Al. (7:25 p.m. U.S. Central Standard Time)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Roger. [Long Comm Break]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay, Houston. We both slept 5 hours. My PRD is 11020, and Al's is 04021. [Pete's Dosimeter reading is unchanged while Al's has clicked on the last digit, signifying 0.01 rad. The counters were not set to zero at the start of the mission so that there would be no doubt as to whose dosimeter was being read. Their average total skin dose for the mission was 0.58 rad, most of it accumulated during passage through the Van Allen Belts on the way to and from the Moon. To put these numbers in context, Journal Contributor Dave Hardin points out that the typical exposure from a chest x-ray is 0.1 rad a

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Rog. Copy, Intrepid. For information, Pete, can you see the ALSEP out the LM window?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Sure can.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. When you get a chance, what I would like for you to do is: they are not getting the readings they expected from the CCIG (Cold Cathode Ion Gauge). If you can, we would like you to give a look-see at it with the monocular to see whether you can tell whether it is right side up and whether the port has been opened or not. Over. [Journal Contributor Ulli Lotzmann notes that the 10x40 monocular was manufactured by Leitz, Germany, and modified by NASA's Manned Spacecraft Center (MSC) Houston. It was based on the commercial binocular version.]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Wait one (minute). We left that in a rather precarious position due to that cable last night, and it wouldn't surprise me if it is not upside down, face down, because that is exactly where it wanted to go.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Yeah, understand, Pete. They've given a command to open the ports, and the pressure has not gone down in it at the rate they expected.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: When we left it last night, Houston, we left it sort of on its back facing about 80 degrees from the horizontal. That was the best we could do.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Understand. (Long Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Unfortunately, Houston, it is on the opposite side of the SIDE, which is supposed to be lined up with my view of it. It does look like it's roughly the same position as we left it last night. But I can't really tell. We'll run over there after we get out and look.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Thank you, Pete. (Long Pause) Intrepid, Houston. I have got a late change for you that came in a couple of hours ago. On the rocks you are bringing back in the jettison bag , Grumman has come through and, along the way, several people have decided that the allowable weight to be stowed in the bags on the deck there should be reduced from 35 pounds to 20 pounds. That's 14 pounds of rock and one 6-pound bag.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: I didn't quite get the end of that. Say it again.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Stand by one, Pete. (Long Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Houston, while you are working that problem, I would like to know if there are any restrictions on when we go over the sill. (Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Stand by, Pete, and we will give you the word on that.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. I would like to go as soon as I can get ready without hurrying. And I've kind of got the suspicion, looking over the Prep card, (that) a good bit of this stuff is done, and it is pretty much a deal of hooking up the PLSSs and going. And I think we are going to be able to get out somewhere around 131:30 to 132, and let me look at the timeline and see what we should be doing then normally. [Pete will go out the hatch at 131:37.]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Rog, Intrepid. (Long Pause) Okay, Intrepid; Houston. That's affirmative, Pete. Whenever you're ready, at your own pace, you can go over the sill. Of course, we do want to talk to you about the briefing on the traverse before you go out.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. I'll give you a call in about 3 or 4 minutes. We have some sprucing up to do; and, while we are eating breakfast, you can give us the hot word on geology. [Bean - (Laughing) "'You tell us this and we'll answer it if we feel like it.'"] [Conrad - "'We got it made.'"] [Bean - "That's exactly the feeling there."] [Jones - "Conrad's on a roll."] [Bean - "He really is, right there. It's just so typical."]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Also give us some word on the families, if you would.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay; sure will. Did you get that on the allowable weight of the materials to be brought back in the (spare) jettison bags being changed from 35 pounds to 20 pounds?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Roger. How far down on the scale is that? I can't remember.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: It's 1 inch, Pete.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: One inch. Rog. (Long Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Intrepid, Houston. They want the TV camera brought back, so I've got some changes to your surface checklist to cover stowing it for return when you are ready to copy.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay, wait one.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: What (checklist) page?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Page 65 to start with.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: We're there. Go ahead.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Down under the block that contains words "rest periods," about the fourth item down is "voice-to-voice." We want to insert in there a step to "stow utility towels from the hammocks in the upper boot box". These will be used, as I will describe to you later, to protect the TV camera when you stow it for return.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Shucks. We already took them out to use to keep ourselves nice and clean.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay. Now, on page 67 of the surface checklist.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Go.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. On the right-hand column under EVA-2 Prep, about the eighth or ninth line down, it says "remove ECS lithium hydroxide cartridge and bracket". Do not remove the bracket. Keep it on the engine cover. Over.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Good idea. [This bracket held the replacement ECS Primary LiOH canister during the trip out from Earth.] [Conrad - "There's two LiOH canister types. There are the ones that were on the MESA that go into the PLSSs, but there is also one that goes in the ECS System on the LM. So I guess it (the replacement ECS canister) was stowed on the engine cover, in the bracket, and that bracket was removable - because one of the other things we were going to do was to throw everything that was used out the hatch. So they want us to leave that bracket on there so we can tie the camera on it."] [The replacem

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Now, on page 77 . (Long Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Go.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. On the right-hand column under "LMP", next to the last step after "Verify circuit breaker," insert a step to open the TV circuit breaker.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Okay, Houston. In other words, you say to turn the TV on to begin with and then before I get out to open it. Is that the plan?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: That's affirmative, Al. I should have made that clear. They want to try one more look to see if something short of a miracle occurred, and then you will open the circuit breaker again before you get out.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Sounds good. Be sure to remind me because it's not on my cuff checklist, and I won't have this one (the LM checklist) out. And what's the latest thinking on that, too?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: You mean on why it didn't work, Al?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: That's right.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: That hasn't been resolved yet.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Man, I worried about that one all night.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Don't sweat it. On page 78 now. (Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Go.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Under the "CDR". Now, we're going to have you use your Surveyor dismantling tool, I guess, on this TV camera - the (bolt) cutters - to get it apart. So add a couple of steps here, Pete, at the end of your list. We want you to cut the TV cable on the spacecraft side of the camera connector, below the adapter. And then stow the TV...

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Yeah. I understand.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: And then stow the TV camera in the ETB.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. We'll remind you of these steps since they're not on your checklist.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Also mention...(Stops to listen to Weitz) That's right, because they're not on the cuff.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Rog. (Long Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Go ahead, Paul.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Now, on page 93 . (Long Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Go ahead.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. In the right-hand column, the fourth or fifth line up, after "Unstow 70 millimeter cameras," add a step to "unstow the TV camera from the ETB and stow on the engine cover."

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Next step. (Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. It's been written on page 97 , Pete. (Pause)

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Go ahead.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Let me read it over here a minute, and I'll paraphrase it for you. We want to fold the TV camera. We're going to stow it in the lithium hydroxide canister (means "bracket").

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Do you want us to pack it with the towels as best we can, huh?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: That's affirmative. And they want it...(Pause) Just wrap the remaining...Fold the handle; wrap the cable around the camera as best you can; and stow it in the lithium-hydroxide-canister bracket on the engine cover and stow it with the lens up. Over.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. Now has anybody checked to make sure that we can fit the camera and all the cables and stuff in that fitting?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: That's affirm...

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: You probably can, but I don't know.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: That's affirmative. They had and...

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Oop. (Pause) Okay. The only reason I wondered is in case it...We'll make it work.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Rog. The lens will stick up. It's been checked out; the lens will protrude up out of the canister stowage about 6 (or) 7 inches and they then want you to wrap some utility straps around the end of the camera to hold it in place. [A detail from a photo taken by Frank O'Brien of a LM simulator at the Cradle of Aviation Museum shows the stowage location for utility straps in the Right Hand Side Stowage Compartment (RHSSC).]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: We'll do it. (Pause) [Jones - "That's a new one for me: that you had some spare straps in the LM."]

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Consider it done. (Let's) press (on).

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. And one other thing, on your tiedown of this bag with the extra rocks in it, they want you to run an additional strap...Stand by one. (Pause) Okay. After you get the bag secured on the deck there between you, they want an additional strap run from the straps holding the bag down up to the ISA D-ring for additional support. Over. [As indicated in the diagram , the Interim Stowage Assembly (ISA) is a set of soft-sided stowage bags on a framework that fits over Pete's PLSS when the latter is mounted on the wall behind his flight station. The ISA can also be seen on the left at Neil Armstron

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. We'll do it.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. That takes care of our procedure changes this morning. I'll give your families a call and get the word back up to you in about 5 or 10 minutes.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Bean
a12a.1290150.text: Sounds good.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: What's the Yankee Clipper doing, sleeping?

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Yeah. He's cutting off a few Z's there. (Pause) Clipper's scheduled to sleep until 131:30, and our intention now is to let him sleep until then, if he does.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Okay.

a12a.1290150.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1290150.text: Okay. I got a couple of messages for you here I'll read up to you. "The officers and crew of the USS Independent or - correction - of the USS Intrepid extend their best wishes to all three of you. They're following your progress closely as you write another intrepid chapter in American history. And, from the blue Caribbean, they wish you smooth sailing on your voyage across the vast ocean of space and their thoughts and prayers are with you."

a12a.1290150.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1290150.text: Thank you. [Long Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip ( 27 min 51 sec ) starts at about 129:25:03.

a12a.1292755.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1292755.text: Say, Houston; Intrepid. I'm going to bring the computer out of P06 and put it back to bed again.

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: Stand by. (Long Pause) [Journal Contributor Marv Hein suggests that, prior to this transmission, Pete brought the computer out of Standby and has run Program 06. This exchange is yet another indication that Apollo 12 was very much Pete's show and that he let Houston in on things when he thought it was appropriate.]

a12a.1292755.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1292755.text: Okay, Houston. I've got another one of those 1105 alarms, which is "uplink too fast". I don't know why that happens all the time, but it does. I'm going to go ahead and put it back to sleep again.

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: That's fine, Pete. (Long Pause) [Marv Hein notes that Pete's actions here are very similar to what he did at 121:34:11 , after the first EVA.]

a12a.1292755.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1292755.text: Okay. It's back in Standby.

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: Roger. [Comm Break]

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: Hello, Intrepid; Houston. I have a consumables update for you, if you want it, Pete; and, after that, I've got some lift-off block data. (Pause) 129:31:23 Conrad: Okay. Go ahead with the consumables update, and then the block data.

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: All right. RCS (Reaction Control System) Alpha is 80 percent; Bravo is 76; oxygen is 76 (percent in the descent tank) and 96 (percent in the ascent tank); water, 47 and 99; and your amp hours (remaining) is 850 and 572. [These values either agree with or exceed the anticipated values listed in a box on checklist page Sur-65 . Those values are 78 and 74 percent for the RCS propellant, 65 and 91 percent for the oxygen; 50 and 100 percent for the water; and 901 and 572 amp-hours for the remaining electric power.]

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: The lift-off block data for Rev 25, which is T13, is 132:11:35; Rev 26/T14, is 134:09:59; Rev 27/T15, 136:08:25; Rev 28/T16, is 138:06:50. Over. (Pause)

a12a.1292755.speaker: Bean
a12a.1292755.text: Roger, Houston. We copied the consumables updates, and here are the lift-off times 132:11:35. 134:09:59. 136:08:25. 138:06:50.

a12a.1292755.speaker: Weitz
a12a.1292755.text: That's affirmative, Al. (Long Pause) Hello, Intrepid; Houston. I have a couple of words on your rendezvous radar self-test and your tapemeter , if you're interested in them now.

a12a.1292755.speaker: LM Crew
a12a.1292755.text: Go. 129:33:57 Weitz: Okay. Your rendezvous radar self-test was good. The checklist had the spec ("specification") values, not the actual values, which is the reason for the difference. They ran through them on the ground and it checked out four oh (4.0, meaning "perfect"). Your tapemeter perilune checks were also good. MPAD ran a solution through on the ground here using the actual CSM state vectors. They had been slightly perturbed, and they came up with the same values off the chart as you did.

a12a.1305927.text: Final systems Prep. CB (panel) 16 (garbled, probably "ECS") Cabin Repress, Close; Verify. (Pause) It's Closed. Suit Fan Delta-P, Open. It's Open. CB (panel) 11 ECS: Suit Fan 1, Open.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, Verify ECS Caution and H2O Sep(arator) component lights (are) On. Be on in a minute. (Pause) Yeah. Okay. Suit Gas Diverter (Valve) , Pull/Egress.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Cabin Gas Return to Egress (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: And verify that the Suit Circuit Relief (valve) is in Auto.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Suit Circuit Relief is in Auto.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. (Pause) Just a second. (Pause) There is your hose. Let me button your flap.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Now, if you'll turn the other way, I'll get your other side.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Just a second. (Long Pause) Okay. (I'll) turn to the right here. (Pause) Better? (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Easy does her. That's a boy. Master caution...

a12a.1305927.speaker: LM Crew
a12a.1305927.text: ...and H2O Sep light, and an ECS light.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Yep. Okay. Now, let me get it. Where are you going?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Down here just a little bit. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Why can't I get that to snap? Can't see, that's...(Pause) Okay, that's all snapped. Okay?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. (Pause) [I interpret the dialog here to mean that Pete has just snapped Al's OPS hose to the side of his PLSS. Although the next few lines are difficult to reconcile with the checklist, this may be the place where Pete changes Al's Suit Isolation Valve to Suit Disconnect, disconnects his LM oxygen hose, and connects his OPS hose to his suit.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: All right. Do you want to get...Oh, wait a minute; one other thing, right here. Got it. I snapped your OPS hose in the side of the PLSS there.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Did you trim this thing out here?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Let me do that to you now.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: And we throw in a couple of purge valves then. 131:07:53 Conrad: Yes, I got the purge valves right now.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [Another possibility is that Pete is working on Al's hoses at this point.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Let me check you. Yours is in. And let me disconnect you from your (LM) suit hoses.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: You're disconnect. (Pause) Okay; that's good. (Pause) [Al probably has just changed Pete's Suit Isolation valve to Suit Disconnect.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: It's not in. You're going to have to do that; I can't see it.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: I'll do it. (Pause) Okay. What you have to do...

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Get it started and rotate it with...And then counter-rotate. There you go. (Pause) That's locked and that's locked; while I'm down here, let me...That's locked. Locked.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Hoses under the flap, huh? Let me check all yours. 1, 2.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Safety's in; safety's in; safety's in and that safety's in. Okay. They look good. (Pause) [These "safeties" are the lock-locks of other missions. Each of the ring locks on the connectors has a safety which prevents the ring from opening accidentally.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Mine is. Okay. Take a drink (from the water gun (photo by Mick Hyde)) and (then) Descent H2O (valve), Closed.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. (Long Pause) Okay. (Long Pause) [They are now at the top of the right-hand column on Sur-70 and the dialog becomes easy to follow again.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: "Vent flag (pause) (will clear in a minute). Don helmets, then visors."

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okey-dokey. (Long Pause; audible click) You got it.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Hold still and I'll put this ( LEVA ) on.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: All right. A bit cool in here today. Give you a little chilldown with this LCG . [As they did prior to EVA-1, they are running the ECS LCG pump to cool themselves down before disconnecting from the LM water supply. They will not turn the PLSS cooling system on until the hatch is open, and they don't want to overheat.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: (Garbled) first, let me get it all down in the back and everything. Okay, hysters (that is, hoisters or self-doffing straps).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1305927.text: In looking at the TV, it appears we'll be leaving the TV off for this, so if you would keep that circuit breaker out and go to S-Band mode PM.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. We'll do it in just a minute. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: (To Conrad) Okay. Up. Okay, Pete; look up.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Houston, I'm sure sorry the TV didn't work. It's a beautiful sight to see Intrepid and Surveyor sitting here on this crater.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1305927.text: Roger, Pete. We'll be waiting for those (70mm) pictures. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Here's a pair of gloves for you.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. "PLSS fan on; don helmet and visors." Okay. "LCG pump (circuit breaker) open." Okay. Right now.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. And you might as well get the TV and S-band reconfigured.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. TV's still out, of course. (To Gibson) Okay. We're going to PM, Houston.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: There's PM and (garbled) (Pause) "Disconnect LM (H2O) hoses and connect PLSS H2O hose and stow LM hoses." (Pause) Okay. (Pause) I'm going to turn around here, Pete.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. And I've got my (LM H2O) hoses off. How come we don't have our gloves on yet? [Because of the difficulty of working with the gloves on, donning them is virtually the last step before cabin depressurization.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Very good. Can't see the checklist, that's all. (Pause) Go ahead and get all snakied-up (that is, get the PLSS hoses connected ) there.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, my PLSS water is hooked up.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay; and I'm ready to do the hoses, (that is, stow the LM water hoses in brackets on the wall behind Al).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Get yours routed and hand them to me and I'll stick them in.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Turn around real easy. (Pause) Wait a minute, I've got to get over there (garbled). Coming over. (Long Pause) (What) am I hung up against?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: I don't know; let me see. You look okay.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: I can't move in for some reason.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Move over my way just a little way.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Never mind, I'm going to do it with these.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: All right. You're kind of hung up on the flight data file. [The data file is located behind Pete's station, on the leftside bulkhead above the place on the wall where his PLSS is stowed when not in use. Linked photo taken in 2002 by Frank O'Brien of a LM simulator at the Cradle of Aviation Museum.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: This is going to do it better anyhow. (Should have) done it that way yesterday. How's that look?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, that's pretty steamy. Here's a pair of gloves for you.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Let me grab that checklist again.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: "Verify the following: helmet and visors, locked and adjusted."

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, you're locked and adjusted. (Pause) Okay, torso tiedown adjusted.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: I can see that you are locked. I can see it. (You're) in good shape.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. O2 connectors . Let me check all yours, then you can check all mine. (Pause) Those are vertical (garbled) locked. (Pause) Comm (connector) is locked; let me see about your water. (Pause) Water's locked. Everything's locked.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, you look good. I've been over these a couple of times, every safety...

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: And I checked your water. It's in; it's locked; pins are flush.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Purge valves are all in. Okay, don EV gloves and lock them up.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, here's a pair for you. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Thank you. [Comm Break. They are now on Sur-71 .]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: The right one of mine didn't want to do it either. Take it off again. (Long Pause) [Donning the gloves was never an easy task. The glove fitted into the wrist assembly fairly easily but, in order to operate the lock ring, you had to grasp two widely spaced tabs with the thumb and forefinger of the other hand, pull them toward the fingers of the glove and rotate the lock ring. Once that was done, you pushed in a lock-lock to secure the ring.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Can't tell whether they're in or not.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: (To Pete) Pull this one open (for me). (Pause) Just a sec. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Why don't you just let me have it?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: There you go. (Long Pause) What's the matter?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: There you go. Now do it; push your (wrist lock) button down.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Doesn't want to do it, does it? There it did. I can't do it with your...(Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: It never fails, does it? The one time you don't want something to hang up (garbled) it's (the bubble helmet) going to start fogging up. There you go; let me look at it.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Everything looks good. (Pause) Can you see that lock?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: I can't see it. (Garbled) That's locked. See this one. (Pause) It's locked. (Long Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: (PLSS) diverter (valve) is Min; (garbled) going to (PLSS LCG) pump on. (Long Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Verify it's locked. (Long Pause) (Garbled) tie this thing.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Yes, sir. (Pause) "PLSS Diverter, Min. PLSS pump (on to circulate water through the LCG )."

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: My pump's On and I'm beginning to be sucked down. Let's get the cabin (that is, Pressure Regulators A and B ) to Egress. [Now that they have their helmets and gloves on, the suits are collapsing due to breathe down.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. The jettison bag is up. (As per Surface checklist page 67 ) the LHSSC (Left-Hand-Side Storage Container) is unstrapped. (As per checklist page 71 ) it's got (used) PLSS batteries (and) Li(OH) cartridges, (food waste, and urine bags).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Put it back on the engine cover that way.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Don't hurry. Let me get my CB (garbled under Pete). [The next step is to verify the circuit breaker configuration on the panels on both sides of the cabin. In the following transmission, Pete is talking himself through his circuit breaker panel ( CB(11) ), comparing the breaker configuration with a cue card identical to checklist page Sur-22 (re-drafted by Thomas Schwagmeier). He starts on the bottom row. Note that the number printed to the right of each row is the number of breakers in the row that should be open. The open breakers are indicated by white dots, the closed breakers by black dot

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: I got my CBs real quick. (Pause) Row 1: One, 'in'. One, 'out'. (Pause, jumping the next open breaker) One, 'out'; three, 'in'; one 'out'. Those (the last three at the left end of row 1) are 'in' . (Pause as he checks rightward from the left end along row 2) (Suit) fan 1 is 'out' (the breaker in the second row marked with a star in the diagrammeaning that he is to open the breaker), Cabin fan 1 is 'out'. Glycol Auto Transfer is all in. (The next three) 'out'. (Skipping the two 'in' PGNS breakers) And (the last breaker on the right end of row 2) 'out'. (Moving up to row 3, working from the right

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: (checking the top row) Three âout' (garbled). Okay; that's it.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Same here. They all look good.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Ready for a Press Integ(rity) check. [That is, a pressure integrity check of the suits.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Yeah. Oh boy, does that feel better (with the suit partially inflated and no longer hanging on him)! (Pause) Got a O2 "O" flag; Press O flag.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1305927.text: Yankee Clipper; Houston. We read you loud and clear. Good morning.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1305927.text: Ah, good morning. (Garbled) Yankee Clipper. (Garbled); the batteries are on charge...

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1305927.text: ...the crew is ready for work; and Yankee Clipper's reporting for duty, sir.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1305927.text: Roger, Dick. Your two friends are moving right ahead. They're just about ready to egress. They're running about an hour and a half ahead of time. They're pretty anxious to get out.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Gordon
a12a.1305927.text: Sounds good. [The remainder of the conversation between Gibson and Gordon is omitted.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Mine decided to regulate at 3.9 (psi) for some reason. [The suits normally regulate at a pressure closer to 3.8 psi. However, the acceptable range is 3.7 to 4.0 psi and, consequently, this is only a matter of curiosity.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: I've got to get my O2 off (to start the pressure integrity check).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Let's time it. We'll reset (the Digital Event Timer, or DET).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: (Garbled) (Long Pause) [Having turned the flow of oxygen off again, they are watching the slow decrease due to breathe-down and minor leaks. A decrease of more than 0.3 psi in one minute would indicate a suit leak. Usually, the decrease is only about 0.1 to 0.2 psi in one minute. On later missions, the astronauts will report the starting pressures and decreases to Houston.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, Houston. The decay checks look pretty good. Are we Go for EVA?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Pogue
a12a.1305927.text: Stand by, Pete. (Pause) You are Go for EVA, Pete.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, I'm going to get my ox(ygen back on). (Answering Pogue) Roger. [Gibson has been reading engineering data up to Gordon and, in the interim, astronaut William Pogue is handling the LM CapCom chores.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. What are you going to do?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: My oxygen's back on. (Pause) There, I got a tone, and an O(2 flag, as expected). Looks good.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Confirmed. Okay, " Cabin Repress valve , Close".

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. I'll get it. [Again, it is easier for Pete to reach behind Al to get the ECS valve controls than for Al to turn around to get them.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Wait a minute; it's not all the way. Okay, Closed. What else?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. I'm going to drop the cabin (pressure) now through the forward dump valve . (Pause) Excuse me?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: You're hung up on something. You okay?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Yup. (Long Pause) Okay; 4 (psi); 3-1/2. There you go. (Pause) Okay. [Under normal conditions, the cabin pressure is maintained at 4.6 psi. They have opened the dump valve, let the cabin pressure drop to 3.5 psi, and then closed the valve again so that they can watch the response of the suit pressure regulators and of the ECS.] [As is shown in Figure 7-4 in the Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report, the Cold Cathode Ion Gauge (CCIG) Pete and Al deployed during EVA-1 recorded the arrival of the vented oxygen. Similar experiments deployed by the Apollo 14 and Apollo 15 crews recorded arrivals in s

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, "3.5. Verify cuff gauge does not drop below 4.8."

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, the suit loop (clears throat) is 4.1...

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: PGA (Pressure Garment Assembly, the suit) greater than 4.8?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Start your watch. [Conrad - "So we did start our watches. He's calling it out. So we started our watches at depress."] [They are probably using the stopwatch function to time the EVA. See the discussion at 115:32:45 .]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: No, that little (garbled) cap popped off. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: And I'm 5.0, and the suit loop is 4.0, and the cabin is a half. About 0.6 (psi).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [The hatch can be pulled open at about 0.2 psi. At pressures above 0.35, if the crew pulled hard enough, they would break the handle without opening or damaging the hatch. Note that Gibson is still talking with Gordon.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Pogue
a12a.1305927.text: Everything looks good down here, Pete.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Roger. It looks good up here. (To Al) Okay, there goes a H2O (flag). Got one, too?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Yup; there it goes. (Garbled) [Cabin pressure has dropped low enough for sublimator operation and sensors in the PLSSs are reporting that the sublimators are not yet seeing any flow of feedwater.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay, cabin is still about 2-1/2; it's 0.25, Al.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Just let her bleed for a while.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: My suit's still 4.9. Why don't you jiggle on it (the hatch handle) a little bit and see (if it will open).

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Probably still outgassing. All right, let her go for a while. Let her go...

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Yeah. Still a little bit more.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: These suits are bleeding down, too. See? (Long Pause) They (the cabin pressure gauges)'re holding at about 0.2. (Pause) Now jiggle it.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Think I can get her now, Pete. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Got her. (Pause) Okay. You hold her open.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: (Chuckling) All that stuff whistled out the door. [Jones - "Does that count as a 'stuff'?"] [Bean - "No, I guess that was 'stuff' stuff (rather than geologic 'materials')."]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Just a second. Got my foot by it.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Now I've got to put this Dump valve to Auto. (Pause) Dump valve to Auto. [With the Dump valve set in Auto, the astronauts could, if necessary, open the valve with a handle located on the outside of the hatch.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay; (does) that Dump valve look in Auto?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Let me check. I can't see. Yes, sir, it looks in Auto.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Now, let's just hold this door open right here like that. (I'll) get my feedwater on.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. (Long Pause) While we're standing here, why don't we jettison this gear? If you'll just back into the corner.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: Just a second, Pete. Wait until the suit pressure goes down a little bit. [The suit is difficult enough to bend at 3.8 psi. As the cabin depressurized, the relief valves in the suits could not keep pace and the relative pressure in the suits increased to about 5 psi. The suit pressures are probably now about 4.5 psi; and, at that pressure, the suits are very stiff indeed.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Yeah. (Pause) All right, leave it (the jett bag ) right where it is. What do you want to do?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Why don't you stick it (possibly the cue card) in the crack here...No; stick it in that crack right there.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: (Garbled) I'm going to get this gear out of here. (Pause)

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: (Would you) reach down there and make sure that my water is on all the way?

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. My water light is out! I have a good boiler.

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1305927.text: Okay. Now. Get rid of this bag of gear. (Pause) Back up. [Conrad - "It's a garbage dump. You just push it (with your boot). It doesn't take much. It's just going to keep right on going. Remember, it's one-sixth g. You give it a little push and it's going to zip right out the hatch."]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Bean
a12a.1305927.text: (LM) Caution-and-Warning status check is okay. [Al is referring to the 'CWEA Status' item at the middle of the righthand column on Sur-72 . The ASC Press(ure) warning light on Panel 1 is on. The Preamps, ECS, and H2O SEP Comp(onent) Caution lights on Panel 2 are on.]

a12a.1305927.speaker: Conrad

a12a.1330005.text: Hey, that's a neat ...Ooh, that's glass! Look at that.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Right next to it.

a12a.1330005.text: Yeah. Here, one at a time. [Pete may be picking the rocks up with the shovel, rather than with his tongs.]

a12a.1330005.text: Make a good sample for them. (Pause) And that piece right next to it, there.

a12a.1330005.text: Okay. Houston, how far are we from the LM?

a12a.1330005.text: Stand by.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: (Laughing)

a12a.1330005.text: (Laughing) (Garbled) tricky. I wish we had...

a12a.1330005.text: (Laughing)

a12a.1330005.text: (Chuckling) Hey, come on, I'm getting tired of picking up those little things!

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Get a big one! There's one right there.

a12a.1330005.text: Get a big what? Here, this one?

a12a.1330005.text: Yeah.

a12a.1330005.text: I don't think that will fit.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean

a12a.1330005.text: No, it won't fit!

a12a.1330005.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330005.text: Pete and Al, we show you 1200 feet from the LM. [A labeled detail from LROC image M120005333R indicates they are about 1420 feet (432 meters) from the center of the LM.]

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: Okay. (Pause) Come on, Al, we're wasting time. (Pause)

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: There you go.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330005.text: Pete, as soon as you finish up there, you can head on back toward the east, towards Halo Crater. No need to go any further west. [Had Pete and Al seen any clear indication of Copernican Ray material farther to the west, Houston might have considered having them go a little farther. However, with time running short and with the possibility that they've already sampled Copernican ejecta at Head Crater, Houston wants them to head toward Halo Crater and the Surveyor.]

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Got it, Pete?

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: Yeah. Wait. Let go a minute. (Pause) I'm with you, Houston. (Pause)

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Hey, good show, Pete; good turning. (Pause) [They are probably closing the Gas Sample and, if so, are having much less trouble then they had with the SESC. a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: There you go!

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean

We got a lot of dust on ourselves and also on the outside of the camera. We kept looking at the lens to see if there was any dust on it and to see if it was going to degrade the pictures. Neither Pete nor I could see it on each other's camera (lens), although the other parts of our cameras were covered with dust. We'll have to take a look at the pictures that we returned (which look okay). If it does turn out to be a problem, we're going to have to come up with some s

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Okay. Let me put that up.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: And up.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Okay. We got it. [Al could be talking about removing the turning handle on the GASC . The design of the top is similar to the SESC that they closed at 133:01:26 . Alternatively, he simply could be putting the container in the HTC.]

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: Okay. Give me one gnomon and my shovel. [Pete is hand-carrying the gnomon.]

a12a.1330005.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330005.text: Here's your shovel.

a12a.1330005.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330005.text: Head for Halo Crater. Sampling at Head Crater and Bench Crater Apollo 12 Journal Halo Crater

a12a.1330926.text: Okay, Pete. We will give you a radar vector on this one. If you will go over just directly east of Bench Crater; and you can continue on east until you are just about directly opposite the LM. And then a couple of more steps ought to take you right to Halo Crater.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Sounds like a pretty good vector. That also says that we are running right into the Sun. Does that agree with you? 133:09:51 Gibson: That's affirmative. You will be running right into the Sun. And (when you get near Halo) directly at your 9 o'clock position, you will see the LM. And then a couple of more steps and you'll be right there.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: I've got the LM in sight. It's at my 10 o'clock. (Pause) You know what I feel like, Al?

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: What?

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: (Chuckling) Did you ever see those pictures of giraffes running in slow motion?

a12a.1330926.text: That's about right.

So you kind of have to tack - or whatever you call it in sailing - 'cause you can never put your eyes up-Sun. You always look to the side, because it's too damn bright. And a good (terrestrial) example, I think, is when you get up on the beach in the morning on the East coast and look out as the Sun comes out. You can not

a12a.1330926.text: Say, would you giraffes give us some comment on your boot penetration as you move across there - what you're doing now, and what (penetration) you had back there at Sharp Crater?

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Oh, it's much firmer here. We don't sink in anywheres near as much. Now I'm crossing some of my own tracks. [They have been on the move for less than a minute and, consequently, are no more than 100 meters east of Sharp. They are crossing the tracks they made in going from Bench to Sharp. Al remembers that he was behind Pete and south, to the right.] [ Figure 10-1 from the Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report shows the traverse. a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Yeah. The toes sink in a bit, Pete, as you push off. You land flat-footed, so your heels don't sink in; but, as you push off with your toes, they sink in down about 3 inches. Your heels are only sunk in perhaps an eighth of an inch.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330926.text: Roger. Thank you, Al. 133:10:53 Bean: ...kick off on your toe. Every time he lands he sends little particles spraying out ahead of him and beside him and everywhere else. They go out to distances maybe 2 feet to 3 feet around him. [There is some very good TV of this phenomenon taken during Apollo 17, especially at the end of the Shorty Crater stop when Gene is running back to the Rover from the east rim of the crater.]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. We're back at Bench Crater. Now, have we gone too close towards the LM? (Pause) (We're) going on the south side of Bench Crater, Houston.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. Now, if you'll just go directly to the east of the center of Bench Crater and then continue directly east right into the Sun; and then at 9 o'clock, you'll see the LM, and a couple of more steps and you'll be there. 133:11:45 Conrad: (A little out of breath when talking) Okay. (Pause) I've got the decided feeling I'm going to sleep tonight. (Long Pause)

a12a.1330926.text: Pete, the crater you're looking for, Halo Crater, is just about the same size as Sharp Crater and should resemble it. 133:12:31 Conrad: (Breathing heavily) I think I have it in sight, but I'm not sure. a12a.1330926.text: Okay. Well, Halo...I wonder if I'm standing...You suppose this is it, Al?

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Yeah, I know. But you never can tell from here (that is, from the surface).

The bag had a short straw attached and, if the astronaut needed a drink, he could reach over and take a sip. Journal Contributor John Pfannerstill points out that "during the fateful 'last' TV broadcast from Apollo 13, which concluded just minutes before the oxygen tank blew," Fred Haise demonstrated the drink bag for the audience on Earth. See, also, pages 92 and 94 in the Apollo 13

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Good thinking. (Pause) Let me look in the map, Pete.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. [Bean - "I'd forgotten that Pete said that. That might have been one of the things that triggered them to start putting drinks in the suits. Plus, they're going to be out longer. And here we are, already thirsty. And I think we would have done better, on our EVAs, if we could have rehydrated. I'm sure the doctors said ' look at the water those guys have lost and they're not performing as good as they could if they had been drinking water.' They don't even know it, but a lot of times you're debilitating yourself. You don't know it, because you don't have a reference."]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330926.text: Pete and Al, can we have an EMU check? [This may be a veiled suggestion that they take a break. On the other hand, Houston may also want pressure and oxygen readouts, not having had one yet during this EVA.]

a12a.1330926.text: Coming. Coming.

a12a.1330926.text: Okay; just a second.

a12a.1330926.text: First time I've worked up a heart rate, I think.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. This is sample bag 11D.

a12a.1330926.text: Okay.

a12a.1330926.text: I think we can get to the bottom of that baby.

a12a.1330926.text: Yeah. 133:15:10 Bean: Funny. Do your hands get hot holding that shovel?

[Bean - "Maybe it isn't that the tool is hot. When you grip your hand around there, then the air can't flow in your hand area any more. So your hands don't have the air circulation they normally do. Or, maybe it's a combination of both."] 133:15:25 Conrad: Yeah. Yeah. I'll tell you wha

Journal Contributor Ken Glover notes that the playmate pictures in both checklists were taken from the 1970 Playboy Playmate Calendar. Doug Bennett notes that the two Playmates in Pete's checklist are Angela Dorian (born Victoria Vetri), Miss September 1967, and Reagan Wilson, Miss October 1967, who is seen in Al's picture of Pete.

a12a.1330926.text: Roger, Al. Sure will. I'm sure he is listening.

a12a.1330926.text: This is Halo. [Thanks to the pictures they took, some of which show the LM, we know that they are still about 70 meters northwest of Halo Crater.]

a12a.1330926.text: Yeah. Why don't you come up here...

a12a.1330926.text: Okay.

a12a.1330926.text: I will get the...

a12a.1330926.text: It's interesting. You know, I think this looks like that material that we talked about the first day in front of the LM. Maybe it runs past the LM down into this area. But it's sure different than where we've been. It looks almost (like) it's more...The material is more cohesive and forms clumps, instead of being so nice and smooth. [During the 1991 mission review, Pete and Al speculated that this phenomenon could be due to the LM engine.] [Conrad - "From here to there (at the LM) ain't all that far. Things went out radially. Again, from the Sun, you wouldn't necessarily see some of the stuff

a12a.1330926.text: (Garbled) go around behind you.

Pete has evidently just placed the gnomon because the vertical rod is well off vertical and, undoubtedly, is

a12a.1330926.text: Okay. Right here. Good shot here, Pete. 133:17:58 Conrad: I wanted to get my footprints in it too, so they can see that.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. (Pause) [Pete's picture of his footprints is AS12-49- 7284 .]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Uh-oh. (Pause) 133:18:10 Bean: Okay, I think I will take some a little further away. Back up a little, and shoot a 15-foot (focus) one if it's okay. [Al's takes three pictures at 15-feet, AS12-48- 7074 to 7076.]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Yeah. I'm going to just dig.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: All right. I will be back to collect it in just a second; let me get this 15 footer.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: (To Houston) Is Halo Crater slightly big(ger than Sharp)...Yeah. (Not true)

a12a.1330926.text: Okay, I'm shooting about four here. (Pause) Okay. (It's) real interesting that this... [Al only gets three frames and the difference may be the first indication we have that his handle-mounted trigger is beginning to malfunction.]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: If you'll get some sample bags and we'll...

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Okay, Pete.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: ...scoop this stuff.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. Let me...

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Boy, it sure is fine; it's kind of like over at the other...at Sharp Crater.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Yeah. Looks the same, except on the surface it just seems...

a12a.1330926.text: Except it looks almost finer.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Uh-huh.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Wait a minute and I'll get you another bag full.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: It's funny though. If you saw this on Earth, you would think it was a real soft dirt that it had just been rained on recently. It is probably the result of micrometeorite bombardment and/or ejecta spray.]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: There you go.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Now, that's a good sample bag full. That's 12D, Houston, the sample bag number...

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Is Halo Crater...

a12a.1330926.text: Copy, 12B (sic).

a12a.1330926.text: ...a shallow crater, Houston? With a couple or three dimple craters in the south side of it?

a12a.1330926.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330926.text: Stand by, Pete.

a12a.1330926.text: Okay.

a12a.1330926.text: All right. Let's ease over there...

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: ...And let's go get some rocks from it and everything. We're seeing it right...We've actually got the soil sample from part of it.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Bean
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. (Long Pause)

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: But this isn't 20 feet in diameter. Is it right on the rim of the Surveyor crater, Houston?

a12a.1330926.speaker: Gibson
a12a.1330926.text: That's affirmative; and, from your comments on the three dimples, we show that you're there. [Houston is mistaken.]

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: Okay. What do you want in it?

a12a.1330926.text: We'd like to get the pan and the double core tube.

a12a.1330926.speaker: Conrad
a12a.1330926.text: (Garbled)

a12a.1330926.text: I can't believe we're at the right place.
